 2.5 stars. 
 I remember reading this a really long time ago and it's safe to say that I couldn't remember anything from it. Not one single thing. So really, it'll be like reading it again for the first time and all the spoilers will be spoilers again. 
 I don't want to judge the book too harshly, mainly because I'm not its target audience, but I can't help notice how things were named. The main character is named after Vladimir (the Impaler), there's another in there named "Edgar Poe" and the road that the Tod family lived on was called Lugosi Trail. Pretty much all of the other vampire novels I've read haven't made such strong references to other vampires in earlier novels. It seems kind of wrong. 
 Plus I couldn't help notice that the the plot-line seems to bare resemblance to Twilight and Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban from the Harry Potter series. I could see several similarities in there, a few being Vlad being half-human half-vampire, his long lost uncle and only family member left returning to him and having his parents dying in a terrible accident 3 years prior to this story being written. It seems that a lot of protagonists go through the grief of parents dying, whether it be in film (James Bond, Batman) or literature (Harry Potter). 
 But since they are very popular series, I'd expect smaller ones to take some inspiration. I've known other books and series do that cough Revenants series by Amy Plum cough. 
 This book went on for 180 pages, but it could've been even shorter than that if Brewer made it. For the first 3 quarters of the book, nothing much happened. Just a discovering of confusing symbols and objects, and school assignments. Oh, plus a murder which really, if you took out, didn't really change anything. I guess Brewer needed an excuse to introduce Otis. There must be more on it in the next books, but there's nothing much Tomas can do about it if he's dead (why did he mark a random teacher anyway?). 
 The author does point out some of his flaws while he's writing this, though. I mean, the vampires hunting Vlad down are supposed to be vampires. If Bathory is such a small town, why didn't they just track them or pick up the phone book like the he suggested? He even writes about how vampires more-or-less created cities. 
 I think one last thing is the whole jumpiness of the timeline. First it was Halloween, then it turned to Christmas with the snow ball and then it was suddenly Valentine's Day. Absolutely nothing must've happened for it to skip so many months and weeks, why wasn't D'Ablo getting frustrated with Otis for taking so long? 
 I probably won't go out my way to read the whole series. It's mainly due to the fact that I don't own the next books but if I see them in a charity shop for a decent price then why not. It's just that these books aren't very long (and obviously not for me) so paying PS6.99 for one for me to read in two hours doesn't seem worth it at all.

I recently read a highly regarded satirical novel from the 1980's and ended up intensely disliking it. I feared reading this (my first Vonnegut, hooray!) so closely on its heels would taint the experience for me. Instead, it made me appreciate how tricky it is to write a successful satire. 
 The back of the book blurb for this babbled about midgets and calypso singers and now I see why. This book is almost impossible to describe. I mean, I could write 1000 words about the religion of Bokononism and Julian and Phillip Castle (LOVED them) and ice-nine of course. But I'm sure you'd rather I didn't. I will say this is a pretty funny satire about mankind and modern science that you'll finish and then realize you are really depressed. Mankind is not meant to have the technology to destroy the planet and one day, we just might. But not in some grand display of intentional nihilistic villainy but rather because we are really kind of dumb shits.

If you're looking for a sexy, fast-paced rock star romance, Wicked White will be a highly enjoyable choice. This was a generally light-hearted story about two people who find each other unexpectedly, during a difficult time in their lives. 
 Our hero, Ace, is feeling confined by his rock star life... overly controlled by his manager, playing songs he doesn't feel in his heart. When he loses the only person who has really loved him, he runs away from it all. 
 While seeking escape in a remote place, he finds a girl who is working to make her own dreams come true, but she too, is facing circumstances that are holding her back. 
 When they first meet, an antagonist relationship ensues as Ace pushes her away, but in the end, they can't help be drawn to each other. In addition, before too long, the past is back to haunt them both and truths threaten what they have only just started to build. 
 Again, this was a quick, fun read. The romance did move fast, perhaps a bit too fast. But overall, this is a good pick for fun, summertime reading.

I normally despise novels with alternating first-person point of views because they slow down my reading as I would have to take pauses to remind myself every now and then that Character 1 is doing this chapter and Character 2 is doing that one. Before I get to the meat of the story, my patience runs out and I give up. When I read Gone Girl, a novel with narrative switches from the wife to the husband, I thought Gillian Flynn was brilliant. She was able to tell a story from two perspectives without confounding her readers who is doing what. You can tell the distinction between Nick and Amy. With Everything You Want Me to Be Mindy Mejia proved that not only two but three characters can effectively tell a story--all sharing the pronoun I. 
 In sociology class, I remember the term "impression management" as the act or skill of controlling the perception of people toward oneself. It argues that a person cannot be judged solely on one occasion because he/she has different roles. Role is the part that someone has in a family, society, or other group (Merriam-Webster). Our professor gave us this example: A person who is a terrible student at school, is not an immediate terrible son/daughter at home. Everything You Want Me to Be is an excellent study of this human nature. 
 The story, on the other hand, is really just a fresh take on unforbidden love. We've all heard about it in the news: former drops dead one day, fingers point to the latter. Although I had known what was inside Mejia's bag of tricks, I admit that the manipulation was downright stronger than I expected. One second she's proffering you confidence that yes you're right, but the next thing you know she's giving you an itch on your scalp that needs scratching. You read on, curious as hell, and the satisfaction that follows banishes that annoying itch. Once again, I'm grateful for being manipulated. (The irony isn't lost to me.) 
 Next to our murder victim Hattie Hoffman, I grew fond of Peter Lund. He is one of the three narrators of the story, and his chapters I enjoyed the most. His witty allusions of literary works perked up the book nerd in me. The other narrator Del was less admirable. He's a typical uncouth sheriff who thinks he has all the power in the world. His chapters made me roll my eyes for quite a lot of times. 
 There are times when the prose made me pause because of its Midwestern beauty. Everything You Want Me to Be is well-written, smart, and thrilling. Five stars!

This is more of a 3.5, but I'll round up to 4 because I'm a fan of Jennifer Armentrout's other stuff. 
 Wait for You is good, but it's just not anything special in the NA genre. It's well written, characters are fleshed out, decently paced, interesting plot... but it just doesn't have the same spark for me that the Lux or Diety series have. 
 Avery is way different from the rest of JLA's heroines. She's skittish and weak and for awhile, it was difficult to like her. She was realistic, but she definitely wasn't my favorite. I tend to prefer strong heroines, the weak ones drive me nuts. 
 Cameron is perfect, but he tends to be too perfect. He's amazingly good looking playboy, has a sexy tattoo and a six-pack, all the girls fall all over him... but the minute he meets Avery he is a sweetheart who turns in to a one-woman man. I struggled to find a flaw with him and I have a hard time believing a guy can be THAT perfect. 
 I found the back story and the conflict between Avery and her parents more interesting and complex than her relationship with Cameron. Cameron chases after Avery like a puppy dog for the majority of the book, until she finally gives in and starts dating him. 
 That said, the story was still cute and a fun read. There just isn't much originality here.

This book. Easily one of my favorite Stephen King stories, and a book that sticks with me for a long time after I read it, every time. He mostly leaves off the shock-and gore in favor of characterization and building tension and dread. The bleak, dark portrayal of what happens to people when you strip away everything but life or death. The Long Walk goes on every year, 100 walkers starting in Maine adn going as far as their feet will carry them. And one wins the prize. 
 Like most of King's work, the characters are flawed and human, and in a way that's what makes this story work so well. There are no people who should win, who must win. There is no shining hero. But as you get to know them all and embrace their flaws with everything else, it gets harder and harder as each character "buys his ticket" out of the walk. 
 The very writing in this story seems to echo the walk - at times interpersonal and engaging, at times dead-eyed and empty, with time seeming to fly by in the blankness.  
 It's listed by some as a dystopian story, but if you come in looking for dystopia, you're mostly going to be disappointed. The alternate history of the story is less a focus and more just an excuse for the story King wanted to tell.

Of course, there are evil vampires in the other vampire books I've read - but the plot usually centers around some really "good" vamps that don't pose a threat to humans at all. I liked that this book didn't have any good vampires. Though the humans weren't all that wonderful either, come to think of it. It was just a good twist for me - and I liked the dark feel to the book. It was nice to switch things up.

Similar to many others my interest in this book was evoked by the HBO show True Detective. Chambers' short story collection was mentioned in different context on various sites as a key toward a better understanding of the TV show. 
 To get this out of the way first, if a better understanding of the Yellow King in the TV show is your motivation for reading it, save yourself the trouble. There are endless resources such as this that will do a better job at it. 
 Do read the King in Yellow if you want to know why it is considered a masterpiece in horror literature and can be seen as a blue print for successful mystery novels to this very day (and is giving one a good understanding of how True Detective is set-up): 
  
 The first 4 stories in Chambers collection are loosely connected via the mysterious play called the King in Yellow which is believed to drive the reader insane. Chambers only hints toward the book/play, never shedding any substantial light on it's content, it's only a dark, controlling, and mysterious force in the background: the key ingredient for any mystery story. The moment you dare to unravel the mystery, you'll inevitably put an end to the tale. Consequently, Chambers knows better than to do so, instead he adds to the mystery. Particularly well done (and readily copied by the popular TV show) is the first story "The Repairer of Reputations". It is left to the reader to decide whether the entire story is just taking place in the protagonist mind after being driven to madness by reading the King in Yellow or whether it's situated in a fictional timeline and the story-concept as a whole is reminiscent Ambrose Bierce's An Inhabitant of Carcosa. The collections transitions with an intriguing ghost story and with prose collection, including my personal favorite The Jester into the final 4 stories situated in Paris. While the final 4 stories are generally lighter in tone than the first, they still reflect and echo many of themes touched upon in the first 4 stories.

Intriguing, interesting, original and fast-paced. 
 At the beginning it 's a bit difficult to keep up with everything 'cause the reader is put right away in the middle of action: there aren't explanations or introductions, we meet associations and characters as if we'd already know them and their reality and how the world in which they're living works. 
 Going' on we learn what we need to know, something will eventually be cleared up later, something else is left to our imagination so it's a challenging reading that requires a constant level of attention. 
 The plot captures you completely since Kate starts investigating and after the first few chapters it becomes very clear that the journey is far from slow and relaxing. 
 The concept of the vampire's degenerative biology is very interesting and every character is attractive 'cause he/she could be the hero and the suspect at the same time (and has potential to become the lead in the following books), they're all very special and unusual people but give out a 'normal' feeling, especially Kate: she makes mistakes, makes a fool of herself, admits she was stupid, and she does the strangest things and the most human at the same time. 
 We sense a lot of things, we're almost there to guess Kate' secrets, about her powers and why she has to hide, what she can't or doesn't want to reveal, but in the end we can't give anything for sure; it is also good to see that magic and wounds require a price, sometimes even high, and that this price has to be paid by every character so that there aren't invincible superheroes. 
 What I like the most is that the authors manage to make us smell a track and then distract us with the same ease in which happens to Kate and her fellow travelers. There's always something unexpected. 
 I didn't expect the doctor to be a stupid, pompous ass, and like the other characters I thought he was the culprit. I had some suspects on Bono at first, but then I forgot about him as long as the story progressed and more characters and events came in. 
  
 Curran and Kate' scenes gave me a lot of fun since that 
 "I crouched and called out, "Here, kitty, kitty, kitty." 
 and then Kate's butt meeting the floor! 
 I love and really appreciate how their relationship grows: there's a spark between the two, but they try to ignore it, then that fire gradually spreads and the sexual tension slowly builds up and they start teasing each other in a way that it's very tasty for us readers! Much more stimulating than the Mine-at first-sight thing. 
 Some details are a little unclear 
 like Derek not taking part in the assault when he's bonded to Kate and Curran freeing him only after that assault 
  
 but unless you have problems with being not familiar with anatomy, medicine, autopsies and relative technical terminology or with some splatter images, the time spent reading this book flies away and you immediately want to know what happens next.

Don't take my 3 star review to mean that you won't enjoy the book. There's a good chance that you will. However, this book is definitely written more for entertainment than for educational purposes. I didn't come out of the end of this book knowing much more than I knew going into it. I do know though, that there is other information and other information should I want to seek it out. I felt that there was more information on recent politics in Honduras than archeological information. Though, that isn't really a bad thing either. I also understand why other findings at other Honduran sites aren't really talked about in the book due to the parties rather being at odds. 
 If you enjoy archeology, then you will probably be entertained by this book. Obviously, it was too early into the excavation of the site to have any real in-depth analysis. This is definitely more the finding of the site and the first foray into it. So there's a lot of conjecture, not much concrete.. yet.. 
 More an adventure book than an archeology book. But, maybe that will be enough to attract the attention of those who wouldn't be particularly interested in modern archeology with its' permits and tediously slow excavations.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The story is told from the point of view of the protagonist Miles. Miles transfers to a boarding school and is quickly nicknamed Pudge by his new group of ragtag friends--including his boisterous roommate, appropriately nicknamed the Colonel, who is obsessed with loyalty, honor, and hating the wealthy kids he attends shcool with; Takumi, the soft-spoken and musically inclined Japanese whiz kid and smartass; Lara, the gorgeous and mild-mannered Romanian exchange student; and Alaska, the mysterious, fly-by-the-seat-of-her-pants, and often self destructive leader of the group. For a while, not much happens to push the plot along aside from these characters' occasional mischief, like getting busted for smoking cigarettes on campus, drinking liquor in their dorm rooms, sneaking out after curfew, etc. Everything is pretty harmless and normal. 
 The book is broken up into "Before" and "After" sections. We the readers, of course, don't know what event it is that separates the story right up until the moment it happens...which is a rare occurrence for me. Not predictable at all. The "Before" chronicles Pudge's experiences with his new friends, as well as his growing fascination with Alaska, who goes from zero to sixty faster than you can blink and eye. It's both exhausting and exhilarating for Pudge to be around her, and he quickly becomes enamored. However, Alaska has a boyfriend in another city. Oh well, Pudge. 
 The "Before" section comes to a close with Pudge, the Colonel and Alaska getting extremely drunk one night, Pudge and Alaska making out with her promising him "To be continued" before she falls asleep. In the middle of the night, Alaska goes out to talk on the phone to her boyfriend, and then comes back into Pudge and the Colonel's room FREAKING OUT, crying and screaming for them to help her get off campus because she "forgot" something and she "can't ever do anything right." With Pudge and the Colonel's help, Alaska drives away...and is in a fatal car accident six miles off campus. 
 The "After" portion of the book follows Pudge and the Colonel's struggle to come to terms with Alaska's death. They attempt to ascertain if her death was a suicide or just an accident, as well as trying to understand the rest of the events surrounding her death. The boys eventually get the answers they want, but it is obvious that things will never be the same. 
 This story is going to be one that sticks with me because it totally came out of left field. I didn't expect there to be a tragedy. Alaska seemed way too...real and full of life and looking forward to her future for her to...just be gone one day.

 The parts of this story are more than the whole. Where this book shines is in the details. Nic's internal monologue is clever and rings true, especially when it comes to her ambivalence about labeling her sexuality and the levelheaded and sarcastic undercutting of her own drama at key emotional moments. While I've never been to a summer geek camp myself, I know people who have and their stories seem to jibe pretty well with this (it's also rather like the beginning of college). And there are some cool possible references to the book's predecessors (Nic's occasionally Harriet the Spy-esque notebook entries, even if they are printed in a stupid handwriting font; and at one point, Nic and Battle lapse into medieval ladies-in-waiting pretending, very much like Annie On My Mind). The minor characters are pretty good, especially the outrageous Katrina, and the (often legitimately funny) geeky one-liners come fast and furious. There's also a zing from a computer scientist on botanists which I would swear was a Stargate Atlantis reference if the timelines worked out. I may just have to like any book which features a teenaged lesbian dressed as Prince Valiant, a boy in eyeliner, and a zing on botanists.

 Yeah, this book had some of the prerequisite features of a New Adult book, hot male MC, quirky, yet hot female MC with a secret that changed her from the person she used to be. One thing I really liked about it, though, and something that set it apart from other books, was that while Ethan was totally hot in a J. Crew way, he wasn't a man-whore or bad boy douche and was absolutely freaking hysterical. I completely loved reading the story from Stephanie's POV, she had a fresh, sarcastic and funny voice but Ethan's POV was by far my favorite.  I loved this book. There were so many things that could have gone wrong with this, but it wound up being an awesome surprise. 
 Catherine Pinkerton is a young lady with a hankering to be a baker. Her mother has other ideas, and pitches her squarely in the path of the King. Already struggling the desire to tell her parents of her desires, Catherine soon experiences another complication, in the form of Jest, the new court joker. Adding the attacks of the feared Jabborwock into the mix, and Catherine's life begins to unravel. 
 Catherine is a great character, you can see her inner turmoil increase, as her desires conflict with those of her parents. Her growth from kindly, dreaming baker, to the vengeful Queen of Hearts, is a joy to behold. 
 Jest is a delightful character, conflicted and funny. His influence on Catherine is fascinating to behold, and he just fits. 
 All of the secondary characters have personality, and there wasn't a single one that felt like a placeholder. 
 What I loved about this book, is the way that wonderland is woven so expertly into the text. You don't need to know the world, but if you do, you will love the insertion of details that firmly remind you of Lewis Carroll's masterpiece. From the subtle, the name of Catherine's maid, to the obvious, the Cheshire Cat, these details show that Meyer has carefully read and understood the source material. Meyer's Wonderland is mystical, nonsensical, yet dangerous place, and I loved every minute I spent there. 
 The ending is gut-wrenching, heart-breaking, and beautiful.

In the years since Justine Larbalestier published this book, it's become the subject of some controversy, much of which owes to Larbalestier being a white woman writing a black main character who is a compulsive liar. A black girl who may or may not be genderfluid, or even a trans boy - hell, it's hard not to read Micah as such, because of her history of having at least once attempted to pass as a boy, and taking birth-control pills to prevent her periods. Because they're just that heavy, but again, it's hard to not read a little deeper into it. Her gender-neutral name really helps with the transgender reading. 
 Larbalestier does, at the very least, admit to her own faults in writing outside of her lane, in numerous posts on her blog. 
 That said, though, she pens a shockingly addictive story, even if (a little similarly to Razorhurst, though this book has a less pronounced case of the syndrome I'm about to describe) it sometimes moves a little too quickly when you want to stop and think about the unreliable nature of the narrator, and whether or not Micah's really telling the truth about what she's recounting in anachronic order. 
 And then there's the paranormal twist. I won't reveal it here - numerous Goodreads reviews happily spoil it, so be careful not to read any of them if you've never read this book - but it's another layer of "is it or isn't it true?" to make the book that much more complex, and it's an arrestingly original take on a mythology that's widely agreed as having been done to death and most literary agents won't take it. 
 It's not my favorite Larbalestier book, not after My Sister Rosa, but for now, it's at least a pretty close second.

I came across Robert A. Heinlein's Stranger in a Stranger Land when I was hankering to read more science fiction "classics" and this constantly appeared in the top five of each list I came across. 
 After reading the initial synopsis of a human, who was born on Mars and raised by Martians, return to Earth, I couldn't help but imagine a 1960's campy science fiction movie in my head. However, right from the beginning of the book, it turned out the story was completely different from my initial imagery (which is not a bad thing...unless you enjoy campy science fiction). Even though I consider myself a fantasy/science fiction enthusiast, I think it's best done when it teeters on the edge of reality, blending reality with science fiction; a thing that this book does exceptionally well. 
 Robert Heinlein's tale follows the initially shy human raised by Martians, Valentine Michael Smith, adjusting to life on Earth. Heinlein's take on what society was when this book was written and what he interpreted what the future would hold is what made this one of my favorite reads: from the government's struggle to have total control over Smith, to sexuality, gambling and alcohol, to Heinlein's take on religion with the Fosterite Church of the New Revelation and Church of All Worlds. 
 On most of his Journey, Valentine Michael Smith is surrounded by great supporting characters such as Jill Boardman, Ben Caxton and Jubal Harshaw (who some might say could actually perceived as the main character). Even Jubal Harshaw's "secretaries" are greatly written characters who help move the story along quiet well. While reading, you feel welcomed into Jubal's house just as Mike is invited into their "family." 
 Eventually Valentine Michael Smith breaks out of his shell, learning how to utilize his powers and become his own man as the story progresses, leading to Smith starting his own religion, the "Church of All Worlds." As the story progresses, Smith learns of the Martians bad intentions for the future of his new home, Earth. The members of Smith's church are taught his methods to advance the human race and potentially save Earth from the destruction of the planet by the Martians. The Fosterites of the Church of the New Revelation believe Smith's religion is blasphemous and climaxes with the bittersweet ending of Smith being killed by a mob for what he believes is for the good of mankind.  
 Heinlein's take on society through this classic tale may have too strong of an opinion for some, or may not seem like your typical science fiction novel, but it is truly one of the greats. It is an example of Robert Heinlein in top form, showing why Heinlein is considered one of the "Big 3" of science fiction authors.

 I described this book to a friend as "X-Men meets Unwind." If that description appeals to you, definitely check out this book. 
 In the world of The Darkest Minds, kids age ~10-13 suddenly start dying. Soon more than half the United States' pre-teen population is gone. The kids who are left are shuttled off to horrible internment camps, where it's revealed that the disease that killed their peers left each of them with one of five varieties of psychic powers. They are assigned a color--green, blue, yellow, red, orange--that signifies their particular power and determines their destiny at the camp. The feared yellows (power over electricity), reds (fire), and, worst of all, oranges (mind control) soon ominously disappear from Ruby's camp. Ruby has been classified as a relatively benign green (basically just extra-smart and logical-thinking), but she lives in terror that her secret will be discovered: she's truly orange, the most feared color of all. When her secret finally comes out five years after her arrival at the camp, she goes on the run. On the outside, Ruby is hard-pressed to know who to trust, what's safe to share, and who on the outside is on the side of the thousands of kids being held in camps across the country and who just wants to use them. 
 This book was super exciting. Ruby's camp is terrifying, and when she gets out, her adventures on the outside are intense. From government agents to an underground anti-government organization to gangs of kids evading capture, the possibility of danger is everywhere, but also the possibility of allies and hope. I loved Ruby's companions on the outside, the little family they eventually form together, and their adventures in the evasion of authority. The culmination of their journey is extra-intense and a little heartbreaking, and I cannot wait to read more. 
 However, I did have some issues with worldbuilding. I find it difficult to believe that there wouldn't be a huge outcry if the government suddenly decided that pretty much every kid between the ages of 10 and 13 needed to be shipped off to "rehabilitation camps," where parents wouldn't be allowed to see their children. Ever. I don't think the government even placates them with something about how they'll be allowed out when they're older. They're just gone. No way would parents just roll over and let that happen. Sure, in the book, there are some parents who hide their kids, but there's no nation-wide outrage, no parents storming the gates of the camps and demanding to see their kids. No way would that be at all accurate. So there's that. (I actually had the same issue with Unwind, but it bothered me a bit less here, probably because psychic powers are less of a morally-laden issue than the delayed abortions of Unwind, which I find even more ludicrously unbelievable.) There's also a lot of hand-waving in regards to the disease that somehow kills most kids but grants some of them one of five very specific psychic powers. And seems to be centered in the U.S., for more hand-wavy reasons. I sure hope Alexandra Bracken has some answers for me in book two, and that the hand-waving in this book was more a result of Ruby being kept in ignorance than lazy writing. 
 Lastly, I just need to say that if someone hadn't pointed out in a review that this is the same author who wrote Brightly Woven, I would never have made the connection. I read Brightly Woven when it came out in 2010, and all I remember is that it's a sort of blandly enjoyable generic high fantasy that involves a heavy dose of insta-love. Bracken certainly did a 180 here! Holy smokes, seriously can't get over the fact that this is the same author. If you read and didn't enjoy Brightly Woven, don't let that prevent you from picking up this book. In The Darkest Minds, Bracken has achieved whatever of the opposite of a sophomore slump would be called. It's definitely worth your time.

 As always we have our adoringly wonderful Ethan. It's always nice to have a change of pace and have a book narrated by a male character.  Next we have Lena, our lovely green eye/gold eye brunette beauty who can also cast all sorts of craziness your way. She was a bit twisted in her own right, which I adored. And although many of her decisions, in my opinion, sucked, I do feel for her, even through her stupidity. After what happens at the end of BC, you can't help but think Lena is in deep shit for some bad stuff. 
 Moving on, we have Amma, Ethan's stand in mother and caretaker, who we find out so many new things about, plus, she has always been a character I love. Mostly for her superstitious ways and for the complete South that is in her. It's one of the things I love so much about this series, the deep South implanted within. Link, Ethan's best friend, is really an awesome friend and I would love one just like him. Ridley is totally nuts and maybe a bit homicidal, which I suppose is why I love her. Well, that and her fabulous wardrobe. 
 I do think my favorite character of all time though is Macon, Lena's uncle. I know he isn't in the book much, and mostly in flashbacks, but his character to me has always been fascinating. 
 Overall, the characters were wonderful and the plot was so surprising that I think the year wait was definitely worth it. And seriously, with prison balls, siren's who lick lollipops, a crazy pack of incubus', a secret love that spans decades, a Siamese cat that RoCkS and the Order of Things you couldn't ask for more.

The Glass Books of the Dream Eaters is certainly an unusual book for the 21st century. A strange melodramatic mixture of Jules Verne, Philip Pullman and maybe a touch of Conan Doyle, it didn't really work for me. The author seemed happy to use 100 words where 50 would do -I felt the book could have been half the size. 
 You've by now heard the story - Celeste (Called "Miss Temple" through the book) travels from an unnamed island, presumably in the Caribbean, to a London-ish unnamed city in an un-named British-like country in an un-named Victorian-like era, meets and gets engaged to and then has her engagement broke by Roger. 
 A surprisingly (to both herself and her ex-fiance) enterprising young woman, she sets out to understand why she has been unceremoniously dumped. This leads her into discovering a plot to extract the minds of the richest and most influential people in the country, storing the memories in the titular glass books. Escaping (just), she is helped two unlikely protagonists. Through many long-winded and over-described adventures, she and her companions survive, eliminating all of the plotters one way or another. Or do they? After 800 pages, we get a cliff-hanger of an ending. 
 Just one of the several annoying things about the book. I found the book alternately annoying and addicting. There were numerous chase and fight scenes, which were over-described and tedious. I also found the not-naming of the places very annoying. But the imaginative concept of the plot and the in-fighting of the plotters was original, as were the three heroes. And the mixture of Vernesque technology brought a mood to the book that was enjoyable. I did see some suggestion that it was like Dickens or Wilkie Collins, but I felt none of that realism they brought to their stories. This was much more Jules Verne or Philip Pullman. It was OK, but I can't recommend it.

This is one of those bittersweet moments in the literary world. The moment you've been anticipating and dreading simultaneously. The end of a series. The time when you FINALLY get to know everything. Every question will be answered. But it also means finality. The end. No more of these friends whose world you've been privileged enough to share for a brief time. 
 For me, The Lost Codex encapsulates all of those feelings. I have been dying to get to this point since i read the first book. And once I had it on my Kindle, I felt ecstatic! I would know who Alice was meant to be with. I would know WHO the Librarian is! But then, I realized that this is it. I'd have those answers, but then no more adventures. 
 It was worth it all. 
 Heather Lyons is brilliant. I cannot stress that enough. From the first time I read The Collectors' Society, I knew she had a gift. And this unique story is only part of it. To have classic characters brought back to life is incredible, but putting them in modern times --- GENIUS. 
 We've followed Alice, Finn, and company to Hell. And now it was a matter of getting everyone out alive. Would it be possible? Honestly, I had no idea. I was anxious to even begin this book. So many things were hanging in the balance. HOW WOULD SHE PULL THIS OFF? In typical Heather Lyons fashion, she delivered. I can't even express just how much I loved this. I can tell you that for almost the entire book my chest was tight. Nothing about this conclusion is dull or boring. It's a helluva ride and worth every hour you spend reading. There is action, adventure, romance, the whole enchilada. Fans of fantasy and the rest of this series should have no complaints. (Well, except that it's over!) I really can't go into detail for fear of spoiling the outcome, but I will say that I found it to be perfection. I do have one question about how one favorite ended up, but maybe another time. For now, I'll relish this story, these characters... 
 I am still in awe of this entire series. I beg you, if you are undecided or hesitant to just give it a chance.

It makes me sad that such a beautifully written, moving novel could fall so short of its potential. The protagonist, Paul, is a grieving widower trying to piece together the events that led to his wife's death. The only witness is Lorelei, a Rhodesian Ridgeback who Paul vows to teach how to "speak." 
 Part of what drew me into this novel were the parallels I could see in it to my own life. But what was the true strength is how Parkhurst does such a wonderful job when describing human-dog bonds, "There is a kind of grieving that dogs do, a patient waiting for homecoming, a sniffing for a scent that is no longer there. . ." And it is therefore such a disservice to the reader that such a ridiculous turn should be taken in Paul's search for a linguistically-capable dog. It is at complete odds with the rest of the novel, and frankly, any decent editor should have known better than to allow this section to remain in the novel.

Wow - I really seem to be in the minority here, people loved this book. Me? Not so much. I'll write why as soon as I've gotten over my disappointment... It just seemed so promising. 
 Disclaimer: I may be unnecessarily hard on this book, but that is only because of its lost potential and my belief that the author is one of the most essential writers of this era. 
 There's no denying China Mieville is an extraordinary, challenging writer. I've personally had a slightly mixed-bag experience with his books, beginning with the beguiling (and utterly bonkers) Railsea before falling utterly head-over-heels with the language of Embassytown. The City & the City was incredible but difficult, slow-going, while Un Lun Dun was a perfectly adequate disappointment, feeling rather too derivative (a younger Neverwhere, perhaps) but still fun. The least of his books, for me, was Kraken, which still felt somewhat too familiar, and not nearly fun enough for its concept. 
 His best works are exceptional, his worst at least inventive. It's a fine line that separates the two, and I think it has something to do with the combination of idea and language. Railsea and Embassytown had both, The City and the City had such an astounding idea that the duller writing was excused. 
 This Census Taker has an idea, but it is hidden out of sight in the corners and crevices of the story. You can catch glimpses of it, out of the corner of your eye - but there is nothing to grab on to, nothing solid to hold. Comprehension is not the end-game here, and this aspect of the story I unreservedly loved. 
 There are ruined cities and destroyed civilisations in the distance. The boy is fighting to understand the destruction of his own, small world, while the world itself seems to be barely settling from its own destruction. 
 I pictured this: 
 Shaun Tan's worlds (this one is from The Arrival) and astounding imageries are a perfect fit, and if this book were ever to be illustrated then he is the only one to do it justice, I think. But for it to be worthy of illustration, this story needs some serious work. 
 The lack of clarity is emphatically not an issue here. It is the pure, physical writing that lets down everything else. I've seen Mieville spin words into gold, pull the most obscure and perfect phrase from the depths of this language - and possibly others, too - turn punctuation into plot and each time capture in all in the most perfect font possible. Language, for him, is clearly incredibly important, and his skill with it is undeniable. So why is this book so painful to read? 
 The constant changing of tenses is awkward, the shifts between first, second, and third person perspectives are hideously clumsy. Since reading this, I've seen reviews that argue it intentionally re-creates the confusion the main character is feeling. The argument is admittedly very valid, and fits with how Mieville tends to write, pushing boundaries. That doesn't mean it works. Risks are essential, yes, and he seems always willing to take them. Risks don't always pay off. 
 This review here, by Bill Morris, says it best: 
 "There was no escaping the fact that I was reading a bad book by a very fine writer, but it occurred to me that this was actually a good thing. China Mieville, a writer with an international cult following whose commercial success is every bit as secure as Murakami or Franzen's, had dared to do something that they, so far, have not. He had dared to take risks, he had dared to leave his comfort zone, he had dared to fail. And that's precisely what he did. I find a failure of this kind far more admirable, if not more satisfying, than another safe commercial success." 
 His other words - those that aren't changing tenses and times and perspectives - lie flat and dull on the page. There is no emotional investment, we are left clinically cold - and not through fear but through apathy. If that was also the intent then I applaud, it worked. But his previous books have shown the ability to create a similar tension without the complete lack of emotion, "cardboard cutouts" and I so badly wanted that to be the case again. 
 As I said before, This Census-Taker has an idea, but that is lost in the experiment. I only wish the idea had triumphed here.

This very well might be my favorite thing that Stephen King has ever written. 
 The Mist is primarily about the way people behave when placed under extreme stress in uncanny circumstances, and since it's a horror story, the answer is "badly." This is a widely-held belief that is actually untrue in real life--repeated experiments show that in the wake of natural disaster, people actually become more generous and compassionate--but it's also about a pressure cooker. In a real disaster, generally the period where people are trapped indoors in a small area is short. You only have to stay in the shelter until the hurricane passes overhead and everyone knows it. The mist is an outside context problem with no precedent, and honestly, I don't think Mrs. Carmody is wrong for assuming that it's the end of the world. If an unnatural mist filled with monsters rolled in and I didn't know whether my wife was alive or dead, what had happened to my friends, and when or if the mist would end, I would probably come to the same conclusion. 
 Different characters deal with it in different way. The workers at the grocery store seize on the generator as a problem that can solved, unconsciously deciding that if they can get the generator started again, somehow the mist would go away. The out-of-towner Norton refuses to believe that there could possibly be anything wrong other than a cloud, probably caused by the strange storms earlier, and he walks into the mist with a few others and is never seen again. Mrs. Carmody determines that it's G-d's judgement upon this sinful Earth, and that it must be dealt with the old way--a sacrifice. And David Drayton, the main character, is the everyman in a bad situation who mostly keeps his head and eventually manages to escape the market, though "escape" is relative here because there's no easy salvation from the mist. 
 That's what I really like about The Mist. Its mood, the claustrophobia not necessarily from being in a place without an exit, though that's part of it too since there are almost seventy people trapped in the grocery store. The claustrophobia of being in a situation with no way out, and how people deal with it. Some of them pretend that it's not happening, some completely give up, some assign some sort of transcendental meaning to everything. Some try to escape at any cost. Maybe they even succeed. 
 A few reviews mention that the source of the mist is unexplained, and I've also heard criticism of the movie for making it clear that the source is the Arrowhead Project, but I'm just confused by those complaints. The source in the novella is clearly the Arrowhead Project. There's no reason for it to be brought up so often, for the screaming sirens all headed north, for what happens with the soldiers in the grocery store, for the direction the mist came from, for any of that other than to point to the real cause. I mean:"That's what they're fooling around with up there. Shooting atoms into the air and all that." 
 "Mr. Giosti, the air's full of atoms," Billy had said. "That's what Mrs. Neary says. Mrs. Neary says everything's full of atoms." 
 Bill Giosti gave my son Bill a long, bloodshot glance that finally deflated him. "These are different atoms, son."This is not a situation that's supposed to be mysterious. 
 There's not that much to the actual narrative, but in terms of creepy mood, The Mist is top-notch.

Following review from The Telegraph by Elena Seymenliyska 
 It is 1937 and Katey Kontent (as in state of being) is a young woman living it up in Manhattan. By day she earns her rent typing depositions at Quiggin & Hale. By night she gets her kicks sneaking into the Capitol Theater or slipping into smoky jazz bars in Greenwich Village. Perched on stools with her room-mate Evelyn Ross, they can make a Martini last an hour - unless, that is, they manage to charm someone else into buying the drinks. 
 One snowy New Year's Eve, that someone else is Theodore Grey - Tinker to his uptown friends. "Dibs," says Eve as he walks in, his cashmere coat draped over one arm, his royal blue eyes surveying the crowd like he's at the helm of a schooner. A round of gin and a bottle of champagne later, the newly fast friends make resolutions for each other. Be less shy, suggests Tinker to the girls, laughing. Get out of your ruts, says Eve, serious. Fortune is listening: before the first week of 1938 is through, the lives of the three of them are changed forever. 
 Rules of Civility by Amor Towles caused a stir last year on account of the sizeable advance paid by the British publisher for this first novel - reputedly PS100,000, offered over what the editor called "a very appropriate midday Martini". 
 Towles, a Boston-born, Manhattan-based financier, set himself the task of writing a novel in a year, with two weeks to draft and revise each of the book's 26 chapters. 
 The exercise certainly pays dividends - the best feature of Rules of Civility is its fast pacing and irresistible momentum. The language is snappy, too, full of period idiom and witty one-liners. "Bust my bosoms," exclaims a boarding house room-mate as she knocks Katey off her heels. "Come on, sweet stuff," calls out a train conductor as Katey idles by the door. "Sweet your own stuff," Katey parries back. 
 Katey herself is another of Towles's bankers. A cross between Dorothy Parker and Holly Golightly, she is a priceless narrator, as well as a memorable character in her own right - the brains of a bluestocking with the legs of a flapper and the mores of Carrie Bradshaw. Her progress from the lowly typing pool of a legal firm to the glitzy offices of the magazine giant Conde Nast and from the low-rent Brooklyn of her birth to a Central Park apartment with a doorman is a classic American fairy tale. 
 Eve is also a classic, in the best-friend variety. A glamorous blonde from Indiana who wants to make it in the big smoke without the help of daddy's funds, she is a perfect chalk-and-cheese foil to Katey, daughter of an impoverished Russian emigre. And Tinker is yet another classic too, a character straight out of F. Scott Fitzgerald, as are most of Towles's men. (The ones that aren't, such as Tinker's brother Hank, an arrogant and angry artist, owe their debt to Hemingway instead.) 
 That familiarity is part of the novel's pleasure: it is so readable precisely because it is so unchallenging. In fact, Rules of Civility is like a collage of the 20th century's greatest cultural hits: a glimpse of Edith Wharton here, a wink towards Hitchcock there, a blast of Cole Porter there. It all feels a bit second-hand, a bit pastiche. For all its sparkle, why have costume jewellery when you've paid for diamonds? 
 ************************* 
 That review about captures how I felt about Towles novel. It was a great escapist read. I had fun and was entertained throughout. Of particular enjoyment - picking out all of the literary references and enjoying Katey's Bookishness.

 R is a zombie. He doesn't remember his name or what he did for a living before he died. He doesn't know how old he is. He lives in an airport with a bunch of other zombies, including his friend M. Every so often they go out to feed, but mostly they just roam around the airport. On one of the hunting expeditions, R ingests the brain of a boy named Perry and suddenly he feels a connection to Perry's girlfriend, Julie. 
 I had been hearing good things about this book for awhile and then when I found out it was being made into a movie I had to read it. Wow, this book was amazing. It is one of the most original works I have read to date. I thought writing it from R's perspective was great. Most zombie books are written from the perspective of the humans being attacked and the zombies and because this one was not it was such a fresh take. I enjoyed the world building, Marion employed. All good sci-fi and fantasy books need that attention and it was great he was able to seamlessly insert it into the story without spending a lot of time on backstory. 
 The characters in this book were awesome. Even the zombie characters all had their own distinct personalities. The story really flowed through the characters. They delivered some of the best and most humorous one-liners of any book I've read. I found myself laughing out loud every few paragraphs. They also tackle serious issues with sincerity and realness. 
 The book, like any other dystopia/post-apocolyptic novel, has much to say about human nature and society. It was very interesting the zombies had their own society, government, and hierarchy. It just seemed to show the carryover of humanity in these inhuman creatures. This book is an easy read, but it will make you think. I highly recommend this book to everyone. I know people hear zombie romance and think its just the new Twilight, but it is a very original novel and a worthwhile read (and I promise you Julie is a much more compelling female lead than Bella). I really hope they don't ruin this as a movie.

With a page count of 416, I expected way more out of This is What Happy Looks Like. I'm convinced that even with 300 pages, the story would've had adequate room to breathe. In fact, I expect a whole lot more depth out of a thicker book, especially when it's Contemporary. There's little world building required in Contemporary, so the complexity needs to lie a lot more in the plot and the characters. Sadly, I didn't see that complexity that I expected. 
 Somehow the characters, while not one-dimensional per se, didn't hold my interest for long. The initial email exchanges were cool and kinda funny too since it turns out Graham has a pet pig but once the book transitioned to "real life", there wasn't all that much left to hold my interest. No twists and turns. Just an introduction of conflicts in the first few chapters that were all resolved in a very predictable manner towards the end. Most of the chapters in between read like fillers to me. 
 The least that could've come out of this would've been a sweet romance that leisure unfolded between the pages. Alas, that didn't happen either. Despite all the time in the world that could've been contained in the middle chapters, I have to cry out instalove! I mean, come on! Graham already planned to spend his week-long break from filming with Ellie practically the moment he laid his eyes on her. Sure, they had emailed each other for a couple of months and so it might come off as though they had known each other a while. All well and good. But the basis of their real life relationship didn't solidify much over the course of the weeks, so what was the point of it all, I ask!  
 I don't mind reading books where readers mostly experience characters' day-to-day lives and no crazy plot twists happen. They don't all need to be issues book with heart-wrenching stories. Neither do they have to be so hilarious, I can't hold my laughter in. I do however require depth in those cases. I want to see what makes those characters tick and why they make the choices the way they do. Even if a book is meant to portray a sweet romance, there has to be something more than just that. There has to be more to the characters and the plot. Doesn't help that a third through the book I thought, "Here's a good place to end. I don't need to read the rest to know what happens anyway." 
 That's why I decided the book just wasn't for me. It was light-hearted yet so incredibly long-drawn and these two things don't go well together for me. If a book is light-hearted, then it shouldn't waste too many words to get to the point. If it's long-drawn, it better be because it's building up the suspense and makes the wait worth it. The combination of these two only makes sense to me if a good measure of philosophising is thrown in or good measure. That obviously wasn't the case in This is What Happy Looks Like. It could've turned out to be a nice little tale to while away a couple of hours like 
 The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight 
 but for that I found it too thick a book.

A very, very good read, and one that I think anyone who's interested in how our society has gotten to be the way it is should read. Malcolm Gladwell confronts two of the common misconceptions that we have about success- both extreme individualism and extreme collectivism- and shows that the truth is both more complex and more interesting. Full of examples and hard data, Malcolm backs up his thesis with both narrative and academic verve. 
 Perhaps most intriguing, however, is how he concludes the book. Is it possible to manufacture outliers? Is it in the realm of possibility to predict what will cause individuals to achieve practically unmitigated success? When the factors that he recounts are so distinct, and in some cases so apparently random, is it really feasible to attempt recreating the conditions that lead to these outliers? 
 If it's possible, then Malcolm might well be pointing the way to a societal revolution the likes of which are practically unparalleled. But therein is the question: it's one thing to be able to retrospectively point out the unexpected causes of a Bill Gates or a Joe Flom, but does that knowledge help us to create the conditions where we can have, as Malcolm puts it, thousands of either? Time and the proper cultural changes alone can say, but sadly, I fear that we'll never learn whether he was right or not simply because we're unwilling to take those risks, or to believe in that vision.

A warning in advance: Those who don't like to see the heroes have sexual interactions outside the main pairing might give this one a pass, since there is an on-page scenes with Andy and someone else, where CK is present and agreeable to, but doesn't take part in. 
 Andy knows that he's a sub, and he knows that he needs hard scenes with enough pain that he can get away from himself. Or so he thinks, until he meets CK and the new Dom manages to make Andy almost forget his own name with only one kiss. Now Andy is completely out of his depth. How can something so simple make him feel so good? How can CK take him to such heights using minor pain, gentle touches, or sometimes without touching him at all? 
 This book surprised me in many ways since it featured a new-to-me aspect of the BDSM lifestyle. CK is mostly about the psychology, the balance of powers. He doesn't force, but seduces his subs into surrender. Often enough, his scenes with Andy turn into something very alike to psychotherapy sessions, leaving the sub shaken to the very core. (CK is responsible enough to point out that scenes can't take the place of therapy, though, he even suggests Andy talk to a professional.) CK takes his role very seriously, even takes time off work to tend to Andy. 
 The caretaker/ nurturer aspect of his Dom personality was in fact CK's strongest trait, something that carried over into his everyday persona. He is even a bit overbearing at times; in Andy's place, CK's mother - henning would most probably have driven me nuts. However, it's just what Andy needs, even though he teases CK about it once or twice. 
 We don't learn much about CK's background. What he does for a living remains some nebulous corporate job, his age isn't revealed until late in the story, even his real name remains a secret to the very end. (Actually, I found him being called by his initials a witty referral to the book's title.) I'd have loved to get to know him a little better in this aspect. 
 Andy's everyday life was much more elaborated, from his personal history to his present job in construction. I enjoyed meeting Jeff, Andy's boss and friend, who is a great guy if there ever was one, and I particulary enjoyed watching Jeff give CK a most amusing ticking-off about Andy. 
 I really liked Andy, who was well-drawn and multilayered. He's a physically strong man, courageous enough to own up to his need for submission. Even though he had to endure abuse, masked as BDSM play, Andy is stubborn enough to return to the scene, trying over and over again to find someone who can meet his needs. Still, Andy isn't above reconsidering what he always took for his personal truth, although it takes someone of CK's insight, compassion and persistence to make Andy see the light. 
 CK, on the other hand, was a bit over the top for me. Yes, he made mistakes, misjudged Andy at first, but once they started working together in earnest, CK almost turned into Andy's larger-than-life, all-knowing savior. He was perfect for Andy, though, and the chemistry between them was as sizzling hot as their emotional connection was palpable. They made for a wonderful, believable couple, and I was happy to see them finding their HEA. 
 I can really recommend this book. 
 The title, Alphabet Soup, by the way, refers to the letters B-D-S-M, which through CK, gain a new significance for Andy.

I've just realised I failed to write a review, which is unfair since I wrote one for the books I liked less in this series, so here goes. 
 I definitely liked this one better. 3, no, 3.5 stars. Once again, I wish we could use half-stars on Goodreads. I smiled and even laughed at some of the ideas. The Organic Food shops. Amazon being run by... yes, the Amazons (it's so simple it's actually brilliant). Arion, the horse equivalent to "I'll drop F-bombs any time, honey". The integration of Roman culture, this time, with Camp Jupiter, which we see for the first time. Terminus, the armless god who keeps flailing his arms somehow. I know some readers will find such things ridiculous, but I guess I'm just one of those people who enjoy a certain dose of over-the-top antics, at least from time to time. 
 Oh, let's not forget the regular injection of myths, and not necessarily the most well-known ones. It made me brush up on my Mythology 101 notes. Pretty useful. 
 The characters: above all, Hazel, who was kind of given the shaft in life. (Looks like the sons and daughters of that one often get the shaft in this series, huh?) I liked Hazel. She was brave, eady to walk the whole road even though she knew how it'd end up, and... it's silly on my part, but that moment when she got the colour pencils from her father, and used them to draw, well... Yeah, that kid got the shaft. And then, there was Ella. I think she was, all in all, my favourite character in this book. 
 The gods and goddesses: I definitely like the idea of their Roman versions not having the same attitudes as the Greek ones. It ties well into beliefs such as "a god needs believers to exist". The Romans believed in them in different ways, and so the gods took on different attributes. It's a bit head-wrenching at times, but Mars, for instance, was a more positive-looking character than Ares, even though both are technically the God of War. 
 On the downside, in spite of those enjoyable elements, I think the "quest format" is starting to wear out on me. Maybe I've read those books too fast (I read the first series over one month, since the local library had it and I couldn't borrow them for ages either), and jumped too fast on the second one? I don't know. I understand it--besides, it's totally appropriate, in reference to heroes and demigods in Roman and Grecian stories--but I'd like to see some variation. Variation, as well as stakes that aren't always so predictable. For instance, I wouldn't mind seeing a character die. Sure, in the first series, Bianca was offed; however, I don't think readers at this point had already been so invested into her, so it didn't have that much of an impact. But if Percy were to die? Boy, now wouldn't that shake things up big time! Of course, it's not going to happen. Still, I'd like to see some important, been-here-for-more-than-half-a-book character getting the boot in a tragic way.

I loved this novella for several reasons: the characters and their actions are very realistic, the cultural aspects and proverbs are entertaining and enlightening, Achebe does an incredible job of weaving this complex story through a simple but elegant prose, and the story itself is extremely moving. It truly is a novella that everyone needs to read, because it can speak to everyone in a different way. Many people do not like the protagonist, Okonkwo, but despite his faults, I found him to be a character worthy of recognition. Most say that they do not like him because of the nature of his faults- he is overly aggressive and never gentle, easily angered and never pacified- but different traits make up different people, and so those assertive qualities cannot necessarily be held against him, in my opinion. You can tell you're getting too old for a certain book when you can read it very quickly. I read this book in about an hour and I shut the book saying 'Give me the next one.' 
 Regardless whether it's a children's book or not, this book is pretty enjoyable. It was entertaining despite how silly it was. But unfortunately there were some problems that kind of just made me cringe while reading this. First, let's take a look at the story. 
 So this book is about three children whose parents have died in a fire and now they have all become orphans with a large fortune that will soon be theirs when Violet becomes of age to inherit the fortune. Because their home burned down and they don't want to live outside of their hometown so they live with one of their relatives named Count Olaf who is the closest relative in town. 
 Everyone has talked about the summary of the book that the author gives us, warning us that the main characters will continue to experience these 'unfortunate events' and that there will be no happy endings. At first, I was satisfied with that. I kind of like books that have situations where things don't always go as planned and bad things do happen. But I think it's safe to say that the ending for this book was definitely a cop out. 
 I'm not saying that it was a happy ending but the book didn't end on a depressing note. If you read the book, you'll know what I'm talking about and if you haven't then you can read the book and find out. 
 The characters are given traits (told to us by the narrator) that distinguish the children from one another. Violet has the mind of an engineer and can build things. Klauss is a reader and is able to absorb the knowledge from the books that he reads. Sunny bites things. 
 Yep, those are the personalities of those characters. Which I guess is fine but those characters don't display those 'personalities' until the climax of the book where they find out Olaf's plan to get their fortune and they try to use their skills to find a way out of his plans. Sunny gets captured as a hostage and Violet and Klauss use their traits to try to rescue Sunny and prevent Violet from marrying Olaf. They do outsmart him but then they can't live with the nice neighbor and have to move with another relative. Doesn't seem sad to me, Olaf didn't get the money and the children are together . 
 The villains are kind of boring. Count Olaf and his men are bad men and do terrible things to the children in a clever plan to prevent the children from outwitting them. But one of the things that confused me was the fact that Olaf's troupe kept telling the children that Olaf was going to inherit their fortune. That is incredibly stupid. Why not just tell them the rest of your plan while you're at it. Wouldn't it be much more dramatic and tragic if Olaf won the fortune before the children knew it and then this book really would have been sad? 
 Olaf. As soon as the book introduced him, I knew there was something odd about the guy. He doesn't try to hide the fact that he wants the children's money and the sad thing is that the family friend, Mr. Poe, doesn't have second thoughts about leaving the children alone with this creep who couldn't be less subtle. 
 Speaking of creepy, that's another thing about this book that's doesn't seem to add up with this story. For a children's book, there's quite a lot of adult content within these books. There are issues such as coping with death, physical violence & abuse, pedophilia, and who knows how many other adult themes. 
 That isn't the problem. My main problem with this book is that if you're going to write a children's book and give it kind of a dark edge (regardless of the fact that this book is for 4th graders) then don't look down on the audience and take it seriously. I mean no cop outs and no definitions that the book feels the need to define to the readers. 
 I'm sorry. I know some people like that kind of writing. I don't. I found it really distracting and unnecessary. If the book is adding adult-related content in its story, then don't you think that the kids reading it are grown up to figure out the definitions for themselves? Or at the very least, are smart enough to look them up in the dictionary. Seriously, it's not that hard. 
 The writing was a pain and I really don't like it stopping in the middle of a description of something just to tell me what it is. So yeah . . . it was alright. I didn't hate it but I didn't enjoy it a lot either. I'll read the next one and see what happens.

This book was the winner of the Young Adult Choice Awards on Goodreads for 2014, and was also part of Best YA Books of 2014 on Buzzfeed. There was so much hype over the amazingness of this book and gasp-worthy shock ending; I felt I had to read it just from peer pressure alone. 
 And so when you're expecting a shock ending to occur, you're going to be constantly guessing throughout the novel what's going to happen. And while I didn't guess correctly, I still didn't react the way I wanted to, gasping and crying with horror. And this took away from the enjoyment of this book, I'm saddened to say. I think the way this book was narrated made this book unlikable as well; it's very fragmented and the protagonist often uses verbs to describe things, which was disconcerting. For example: 
 "His nose was dramatic, his mouth sweet. Skin deep brown, hair black and waving. Body wired with energy. Gat seemed spring-loaded. Like he was searching for something. He was contemplation and enthusiasm. Ambition and strong coffee. I could have looked at him forever." 
 I can just see all those underlines that appear under improper sentences on Microsoft Word! 
 Anyway, I should get on with the story. It tells the story of Cadence (or Cady) who has been going to Beech wood Island every summer with her aunts, grandparents and cousins. Gat, her aunt's husband's nephew has been coming to the island since she was eight, and now, at age seventeen, has become a love interest for her. However, during the summer she went to the island when she was fifteen (known as summer fifteen), Cady has a terrible accident which leaves her with horrible migraines and amnesia, as she can't remember what happened directly before or after the accident, only what her mother and family members tell her (which she always forgets the day after). When her doctors suggest she stay away from the island for a while, Cady doesn't return until summer seventeen, where she's determined to find out what happened once and for all. 
 It's really hard to review a book like this where the big reveal is the most exciting part of the whole novel yet can't be revealed. It focuses mainly on Cady recovering her memories, as well as her relationship with her cousins and Gat, whom she calls the Four Liars (although it's never explained why they're liars). The Four Liars are Cady, Gat, Johnny and Mirren. The four of them spend the majority of Summer Seventeen together, when Cady isn't lying in bed suffering her migraines. Her romance with Gat returns just as it was in summer fifteen. However, she can't understand why nobody will help her recover her memories or why they sometimes insist on doing things separately. 
 If Cady isn't with her older cousins, she's with her mother, Penny, her aunts Bess and Cassie, her younger cousins and her grandfather. We don't get a lot of screen time with these other characters so we don't get any development from them - we just know that the adults really enjoy their wine, her grandfather often gets confused, and the little's... enjoy what younger kids do - playing Lego or reading. I wish the author had spent a little bit more time fleshing out those characters, especially near the end of the book. I would've felt more connected to them if I could actually see a change in them. 
 I think the best part of the novel was Cady's relationship with her cousins, especially Gat. You could tell straight away that when the four of them get together the rest of the world slips away and it doesn't matter that once summer is over, they'll all go back to their "real lives": when they're on Beech wood Island the only important thing is spending as much time together as possible and just having fun. Cady and Gat's relationship was back and forth: "I love you, I hate you, tell me what happened, I'm sorry, I can't, I love you, I know." It would make you pull your hair out and yet I felt the relationship was still somewhat believable, especially as they were only seventeen and they only saw each other once a year. 
 Overall, I think the hype over this book was more exciting than the book itself. I can't believe it was the winner of so many best books of the year awards, as I've read many more books that were more exciting and gasp-worthy than this one. If you're going into this book expecting an amazing bestseller, you will be disappointed. Just sit back try and forget that there's supposed to be a shock ending.

This review is relatively spoiler free.. but if you don't want to know ANYTHING about this or Feed... look away now. 
 Initial Thoughts. 
 WHAT IS WITH THE ENDINGS OF MIRA GRANT'S BOOKS? And, what was that? We have to wait for months until the next book comes out?! COME ON. 
 High points. 
 Shaun. (S)He's hearing voices. Less of the technical jargon for simpletons like me. More zombie action. Things are rotten in the state of... um, America. Underground scientists. The Academy Award for Best Supporting Cast goes to... 
 Low points. 
 I have one major low point.... But I can't tell you what it is because it will spoil everything. I'm such an advocate for not spoiling books and films because finding out what happens at the end of something you've wanted to read/watch really is the second worst thing that can happen (first is when someone pokes you in the side when you're mid-stretch.) I believe it should be Forbidden. 
 Hero. 
 Shaun is just as HOT as he was in the first book, but now he's narrator we get to see a lot more of him and the depths that Grant adds to his character just makes me love him even more. Even though I was sort of won over by George as narrator in the final few chapters of Feed, I thought Shaun was a better narrator and injected a bit more character into the series. I just really loved how Grant created a completely other side to Shaun in this book. I want to say soooo much more but I won't. 
 Supporting Cast. 
 YES. The minor characters in Feed take a step forward in Deadline and become much more prominent and I loved it. They all added so much to the story and the feel of the book and I think they all had great chemistry with each other. Loved this aspect of the book because I think it kind of opened the world up a bit so we could learn a bit more how the Rising affected other people. Also... I have to mention Mahir, the bumbling, long-suffering English gent who loves tea and whose complaints about the things that he has to do go ignored. Pfft, Americans and their stereotypes. *snorts into her cup of tea while complaining about the weather and reading ridiculous tabloid stories about Kate Middleton's fashion sense* 
 Baddie. 
 *zips mouth* 
 Theme Tune. 
 Zombie- The Cranberries. 
 OK, we get it...there are zombies in this book and this is perhaps the most obvious song and also... the troubles in Ireland have NOTHING to do with this book. 
 BUT- I chose this song for three reasons. 
 1)OK, it's called Zombie. 
 2) If you've read this book you will know the chorus is particularly important. Sob. 
 3) The soothing vocal chords of Dolores O'Riordan will help you get through the emotional anguish this book puts you through. 
 Angst Scale. 
 16/10. That's right. THIS BOOK DEFIES THE RULES OF MATHEMATICS. But as to why... *locks mouth and throws away key* 
 Recommended For. 
 People who have read Feed. Basically. And also people who thought anyone who was shocked at the ending of Feed was for sissies. TRY THIS ONE ON FOR SIZE. 
 I literally can't believe we have to wait a year.... A WHOLE YEAR... for the next book to come out. Why? WHY DO YOU HATE US, MIRA GRANT? 
 *twitches*

SO many reasons to love and to hate this book. I'll start with hate, mostly because I can pin those reasons down better. 
 First and foremost, I do not abide books with numerous punctuation errors. The occasional missing or wrong word, I understand. It happens. But there were a lot. A LOT a lot. Editors are employed for a reason. There is absolutely no reason for the multitude of mistakes in this book. Readers should be insulted, as I know I am, that common things like punctuating dialogue properly couldn't be achieved. We should have higher standards. 
 Then, though I found Travis as a character engaging, ONLY in the realm of fantasy should his behavior be okay. I sincerely hope girls aren't reading this and thinking they want a Travis. Because guys like him exist. Only, in reality, their end-all-be-all isn't to protect their girl. And sometimes, when a violent guy is drunk, he doesn't care (until morning) who his fists connect with. Being a live wire who beats the tar out of people all the time is dangerous. Danger is sexy. When safely tucked into Fantasyland. Real life is a different story. 
 (climbing down from my soapbox) 
 Now, what I loved. 
 I devoured it in less than 24 hours. It has a sink-its-teeth-in-like-a-pit-bull quality not that many books have. But why? It had to be Travis Maddox. Travis is a train wreck, but he just has "more". Some people have that unexplainable something, that charisma. I actually believed all those girls wanted him. I have "I Can't Get No Satisfaction" stuck in my head. A fictional character did that to me. Now THAT'S charisma. 
 The title is perfect for the story. 
 Abby's twist was pretty cute. I expected her dad to be a rock star and she toured with him or something, but the reality was way more interesting. She had moxie (with Travis, anyway) and I could believe that she was being herself toward the end and was trying to be someone else in the beginning. 
 There are people in this world we connect with more than others, who make us feel more than others. I thought that was perfectly depicted with Abby and Travis. They couldn't stay away from each other. And though it's hopeful-optimist garbage, it exists and it read as real here. 
 Did I like the ending? It's a romance. That ending was inevitable. If you're knocking that ending, you didn't realize the kind of book you were getting yourself into.

I'll put my hands up and say that I gave up with this book when I was about three quarters of the way through it, possibly more, possibly less. I don't think it's worth my checking. This was for a few reasons, but one stands out to me: I bought the book expecting one thing and got something completely different. 
 I'm a self-confessed fantasy book addict. I love them. I breathe them. Naturally, my standards are high. But I never, ever fail to finish a book. It's quite simply not something I do, period. This has been a big year for me at school and I therefore haven't the time to read as much as I usually do. As a result of this, I've been very selective in what I choose to read. This made it to my list. I was terribly disappointed. 
 Why? 
 The Plot 
 The plot, I must admit, had serious potential. Set in a fantasy land all to do with compass points, Katsa, our main protagonist, is a Graced girl who is forced to work for her pretty evil uncle, the King. She's got to do some pretty gruesome things for him just because he orders her to do it. I liked this idea generally, but the 'gorier' parts seemed very forced and I wouldn't have made them as central as they became. Along the way she meets Po, a disguised prince from another territory with whom Katsa strikes up a romantic relationship, which again felt forced and out of place). The story followed them as they tried to unravel a mystery situated in one particular territory. I didn't finish, but from the reviews I've read, I presume they succeed. 
 I have to say that loved the idea of Gracelings (generally speaking, these are people with abilities such as fighting, dancing, mind reading etc. that separate them from others). It was probably what drew me to the book in the first place (hello, fantasy lover, of course). Katsa was, Graced with killing, which is later revealed to be untrue. Now, you have no idea at how much this buzzed me. I didn't like Katsa, (I'll talk about that later) but I loved her Grace. It was the thing I look for in a lot of fantasy characters; the thing that sets her apart; that makes her who she is; that creates problems for her. But the thing is that, to me, she didn't face the problems that she came against. She just ran away from them. For further betrayal of the reader, check the spoiler. Her Grace of killing, which is, to an extent, a major flaw, is taken away and replaced for survival skills. I'm sorry, but that's just not what I'm looking for in my characters. A note to authors, don't change your characters; develop them.
