What a gorgeous setting for a classic fairy tale story! "Ash" is a retelling of Cinderella set, shockingly enough, in the actual setting and time period of the classic Cinderella story, but with a young woman falling in love with the king's huntress rather than Prince Charming. I was really excited to read this, since YA is still lacking in good stories with LGBT characters, especially in fantasy. And Malinda Lo did not disappoint. 
 "Ash" follows the basic concepts of Cinderella- Ainsling is a young girl living in Rook Hill with her mother and father, growing up loving the fairy tales told by her mother, especially ones about young girls lured by the magic of fairies. Ash's mother dies and her father marries the selfish Lady Isobel, giving Ash two snotty stepsisters, Ana and Clara. Ash's father soon passes away, leaving Lady Isobel with his debts- and Ash. Ash is delegated to a servant's job, her only refuge the deep magical woods, where she meets a handsome fairy, Sidhean. Eager to escape her miserable life, she forms a bond with Sidhean, going against the tales about fairies being tricky and conniving. 
 Ash then meets Kaisa, the strong and talented King's Huntress, and she is immediately enthralled. When Kaisa asks Ash on a hunt, Ash must makes compromises to go, including a deal with Sidhean. If he keeps granting her wishes, she belongs to him. And this doesn't bode well as Ash begins to fall in love with Kaisa. 
 I loved the beautiful fantasy imagery of the novel, as lovely and sweet as any childhood fairy tale. The romance between Ash and Kaisa was also very sweet and innocent, but believable. "Ash" is a great novel for pre-teens, straight and LGBT alike, because it is a fresh, pretty, and more inclusive twist on a classic story we all know and love. It was a quick read and I think that it was aimed at a lower reading level than YA, but I really enjoyed it. It isn't the type of retelling you often see.

Well-loathed books I've re-read 
 Rating: 4 very annoyed, crow-feathered stars out of five 
 The Book Report: No. Seriously. If your first language isn't English, or if you're like nine years old, you might not know the story. Note use of conditional. 
 My Review: All right. All right, dammit! I re-read the bloody thing. I gave it two stars before. I was wrong-headed and obtuse and testosterone poisoned. I refuse to give it five stars, though. Look, I've admitted I was wrong about how beautiful the writing is, and how amusing the story is. Don't push. 
 Stephen Sullivan, who rated this with six stars of five, is now on a summer travel break from Goodreads, so I can publish this admission: He was right. It is a wonderful book. I had to grow into it, much as I had to grow into my love for Mrs. Dalloway. But now that I'm here, I am a full-on fan. 
 Deft is a word that seems to have been created for Austen. She writes deftly, she creates scenes deftly. She isn't, despite being prolix to a fault, at all heavy-handed or nineteenth-century-ish in her long, long, long descriptions. She is the anti-Dickens: Nothing slapdash or gimcrack or brummagem about her prose, oh nay nay nay. Words are deployed, not flung or splodged or simply wasted. The long, long, long sentences and paragraphs aren't meant to be speed-read, which is what most of us do now. They are meant to be savored, to be treated like Louis XIII cognac served in a cut-crystal snifter after a simple sole meuniere served with haricots verts and a perfect ripe peach for dessert. 
 The romantic elements seem, at first blush, a wee tidge trite. And they are. Now. Why are they? Because, when Miss Jane first used them in Pride and Prejudice, they worked brilliantly and they continue so to do unto this good day. Why? Because these are real feelings expressed in a real, genuine, heartfelt way, as constrained by the customs of the country and times. And isn't that, in the end, what makes reading books so delicious? I, a fat mean old man with no redeeming graces, a true ignorant lower-class lout of the twenty-first century, am in full contact with the mind, the heart, the emotional core of a lady of slender means born during the reign of George III. 
 You tell me what, on the surface of this earth, is more astonishing, more astounding, more miraculous than that. Jane Austen and I Had A Moment. She's Had A Moment with literally millions of English-speakers for over 200 years. She's had moments with non-English speakers for more than a century. Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy are cultural furniture for a large percentage of the seven billion people on the planet. (Large here is a relative term. Less than one? Still amazing for a book 200 years old.) 
 Reading is traveling in time, in space, but most importantly inside. Inside yourself, inside the characters' emotions, inside the author's head and heart. It is a voyage of discovery, whether you're reading some bizarro mess, Dan Brown's mess, religious tracts, Twilight, whatever. You-the-reader are going somewhere in a more intimate contact than you-the-reader have with any other being on the planet. Movies, TV, sex, none of them take you as deep into the essence of feeling and emotion as reading does. And no, snobs, it does NOT matter if it's well written, it matters that the book speaks to the reader. (Sometimes, of course, what one learns is how very shallow and vapid some people are...I'm lookin' at you, Ms. Fifty Shades.) 
 So I thank that rotten, stinkin' Stephen-the-absent Sullivan, safe in the knowledge he won't see me admitting this, for reminding me to live up to my own goal of remaining open to change. I heard him yodeling his rapture, and I revisited the book, and I learned something valuable: 
 Only admit you're wrong when the person you don't want to embarrass yourself in front of isn't around to see.

A masterpiece! 
 I can't let it go with just one word, and I hope I'll be coherent with my thoughts. 
 Like with any 5-star book, I'm always overwhelmed with words to rave about this. So first, this is the perfect ender. Second, it's very consistent with the first two books. Third, the author's excellent writing style with an effective first person point of view made this another page-turner. There's more... 
 The story picked up where the second one left off. So Katniss and Peeta are just pawns in someone's or some people's games and while this has lesser action and more plotting and planning, Gale is more prominent here and for a while there I was happy. District 13 was introduced - the president, the rules, the schedule, all screaming war preparations. The suspense and anxiety are still there, the characters' mental degradation described to a fault, but where there is destruction, there's also new life. 
 This book held a lot of emotion, most prominent was angst. There were times I got teary-eyed when she mentions Cinna, because his character grew on me too. I also appreciated her shallow but kind-hearted prep team. I was annoyed with President Coin and all the others who think they others' lives. There's also the nagging question of who Katniss would end up with. I liked the touch of romantic love at a time of war because for just a few moments, they are humans, not killing machines. 
 Katniss's feelings and beliefs were in shambles. Ms Collins wrote a very convincing conflict and some resolutions to the story. I always felt she would choose Gale, but we can't choose whom we love and in the end she ending up with Peeta was justified. 
 "That what I need to survive is not Gale's fire, kindled with 
 rage and hatred. I have plenty of fire myself. What I need is the dandelion in the spring. The bright yellow that 
 means rebirth instead of destruction. The promise that life can go on, no matter how bad our losses. That it can 
 be good again. And only Peeta can give me that." 
 As I see it now, they were meant to be together from the beginning. They complement each other so well, Peeta is very intuitive when it comes to Katniss, and he remembers the small things. Even when things were hopeless between them in this story, they didn't back out on each other, and I'm just glad it's the way things ended. What's more is I appreciate the tragedy, the losses, and all the other mishaps because that's what made the characters stronger - although initially because of the loss, the character wants to die, but eventually, it makes one appreciate life more, and live it. 
 This book isn't just about a 17-year-old girl who's the symbol of a revolution, who fights for her loved ones, but it's about life and death, living and dying, and the lengths people do to survive. The author gave a balanced tone of things; the overall tone is heavy but there are other "breaks" from this. 
 On a different note, the author wrote a small-scale war scenario - what it does to citizens, how it affects them physically, emotionally, and mentally, and the repercussions. It depends on one's point of view how to live life and how one sees differently. This book is definitely a keeper and I highly recommend this trilogy to anyone who wants a great read.

In short: Etiquette & Espionage gets the plot, characters, and whimsical tone just right and I am now smitten with Gail Carriger. 
 So, I may have a new author crush. Gail Carriger is best known for her Parasol Protectorate series and while I always hear amazing things about it, I am, as always, wary when it comes to adult books. When I heard she would be writing a new YA series - set in the same universe as her Parasol Protectorate series - and when I saw the absolutely STUNNING cover for Etiquette & Espionage, I knew I needed to read it. And that's when I found out that Gail Carriger is a brilliant and clever author with a talent for humourous writing, vibrant characters, and fast-paced entertaining plots. And I was smitten. 
 Etiquette & Espionage is like a parody of a Victorian Era novel, complete with over exaggerated ideals of strict morality, restrained sexuality, and refined sensibilities. When Sophronia, a young lady of fourteen years, is picked to attend Mademoiselle Geraldine's Finishing Academy for Young Ladies of Quality, what she doesn't know is that it is no ordinary finishing school. She is to learn to be an intelligencer - Victorian Lady-style. 
 It is beyond me how hours upon hours of class time could be spent just to master the art of fainting gracefully, fluttering eyelashes seductively, and blushing prettily on command, but that makes up the bulk of Sophronia's schooling, along with history classes with her vampire professor and fighting classes with her werewolf professor. Hilarious. I feel like it takes serious skill to get whimsy right as an author. Because anyone can do weird and silly, but whimsy takes a certain amount of cleverness and Gail Carriger got it just right. 
 As you might imagine by the humourous tone of the plot, the characters are similarly quirky and cartoonish and all together brilliant. They have names like Mrs. Barnaclegoose, Lord Dingleproops, and Mr. Shrimpdittle (snort). I seriously LOVED every single one of them. Sophronia is a bold and sensible protagonist who is well suited to a career as an intelligencer due to her curious and adventurous tendencies. All secondary characters that make up her ragtag group of friends are similarly loveable and memorable. There is the barest hint of a playful romance blossoming in Etiquette & Espionage that is sure to develop over the course of the series, involving Sophronia and a guy nicknamed Soap who is - GASP - black. And a lower class sootie to boot! Scandal. 
 It is possible that had I been in a more critical mood, I might have found some fault with Etiquette & Espionage. But I was in the exact mood for it and honestly, Etiquette & Espionage isn't a book that takes itself seriously so the reader shouldn't either. I admit some bias in my love for Etiquette & Espionage because it had a vague semblance to Harry Potter - a quirky boarding school, fun and cartoonish characters, a general whimsical atmosphere. Sounds good, right? You should read it!

This doesn't quite merit 4 stars, but I'm going to round up in this case.

 Unfortunately, a story needs more than strong bones--it needs flesh, and that's what seems to be lacking here. I was constantly left with the feeling that there were scenes missing, that there was more development going on than was actually on the page. Consequently, when the heroine plunges off, virtually unprepared, to rescue her mentor, my immediate reaction was, "What? Not yet!" This lack of prior development robs the major part of the book--her metaphorical journey--of some of its impact.

As a rule, I enjoy the books featuring the SnowDancer wolf pack, so I expected to like this one, and I did, quite a bit too, but not as much as the other SD books. 
 My favorite parts were the parts with Hawke and Sienna, which were so ridiculously cheesy and utterly adorable. I loved every second of their on-screen time. They're adjusting to mated life, and it is so cute to watch. We also get to spend time with just about every SnowDancer who's ever been mentioned, which was a great treat for me. Their pack dynamics are just fantastic. Riley and Mercy's news was awesome and I cracked up at he and Hawke getting drunk. Mercy's a bit more likeable now that she hangs with the wolves. And Hawke is so silly he makes my heart sing. Love that wolf! 
 Okay, Riaz and Adria. I enjoyed very much this journey of two broken people healing each other and then unexpectedly becoming indispensable to each other, and it was awesome seeing their pack help them along the way. It was only in the last 20% or so of the book that their story finally started to really engross me. I think Ms. Singh handled it so well, and I love the emphasis on choice (i.e. that mating is not automatic; you have to make a conscious decision) and the noting of the fact that it's not only mated changelings who can have a fulfilling life, that humans who love each other can have just as fulfilling a life as mated changelings. It felt like an affirmation of love and humanity and it was awesome. That final scene with Riaz and Adria drove home the point wonderfully; it was poignant and amazing. 
 BUT! As I was reading I realized I wasn't ready for this story. I love SD and all the lieutenants have grown on me, so my excitement has been building ever since Ms. Singh announced that she'd be writing Riaz's story. I was sure I would enjoy it, and I did. However, he and Adria really only appeared on the scene in Indigo and Drew's story, 2 books ago. I felt like I hadn't had time to get to know them and be invested in them, so I was actually more caught up in other things: Hawke and Sienna's sheer adorableness, noticing how awesome Riley is, enjoying SD pack dynamics, paying attention to the Psy drama and the tension in the PsyNet.... just about everything else except for the main couple. They weren't strong enough to carry the book because I hadn't had time to know them before they were thrown together. For this book to have worked better, I think Riaz and Adria should have been introduced much sooner, or their story to have come later. 
 The next ARC of the series promises to be interesting. This ride is far from over. Recommended read, even though the whole is a teensy weensy bit less than the sum of its parts.

Ever meet someone at a party and think they're pretty cool until they let something slip and you realize they may in fact be bat-shit psycho? That's how Lou Ford, the protagonist of The Killer Inside Me is. I also suspect that Jim Thompson may have been that way as well. 
 The Killer Inside Me is the story of Lou Ford, a small town sheriff who's a little slow and a little boring. Or he would have you believe. Lou Ford spends most of his time keeping the sickness inside him in check. Lou's a sociopath and has killed multiple times in the past. Lou tries to get even with a man he suspects killed his brother and gets himself ensnared in a criminal investigation. Can he murder his way out of it? 
 The story itself is pretty simple. Ford tries to set something up to sully the good name of the Conway family and chaos ensues. What makes it work is Jim Thompson's writing. Just like in Population 1280, Jim Thompson uses an unreliable narrator and plays it to the hilt. The writing is bleak, powerful, and unsettling. Like I said earlier, Thompson writes sociopaths a little too well for comfort. Sometimes you wish you could warn the characters that Lou Ford is a runaway train and they're standing on the track. 
 From beginning to end, this was one of the more disturbing books I've ever read. If you like noir, it doesn't get much noir-er then this.

 Tomorrow Land is... an interesting book, that's for sure. It hooked me almost right away, and the whole alternating chapters (first chapter, then second chapter is four years later, then back four years for chapter three, chapter four back to four years later...) threw me off at first because I was SO confused what was going on! However, there were a lot of points I liked and it kept me up at night reading because I could NOT wait to find out what was going to happen! 
 I did not like the whole alternating chapters for the most part; there were a few I liked, since it added character development, especially between Peyton and Chase and we got to see their relationship progress before the apocalypse and after, but for the most part I felt like the past chapters had nothing to really add to the story besides filler. The present chapters are the most thrilling parts, and when it would end in a chapter, I knew what was going to happen: we were flung back to the past and I would have to speed read through that chapter to find out what was happening to Peyton and Chase. 
 I liked the drug addiction Chase had--it made him feel more real, because let's face it, you are BOUND to do something if the apocalypse happens and you lose your entire family. 
 Peyton bothered me at times; mostly, in the beginning when she acted like this snotty girl. I also had a HARD time believing the four-year bomb shelter thing. 1) if you are underground for long periods of times, it affects you big time. You need vitamin D (from sunlight!) to live and I am *pretty* sure you will get burned if you step outside in the SUN for the first time in four years in just a tank top. And yet... no mention. Also, I know Peyton has ocular implants, but surely her eyesight is affected by living in a shelter then stepping out in natural light? RIGHT?! Or am I the only one who thinks like this? 
 I liked Peyton's dad's motivations behind this all. I can't say what they are, since it'll be a spoiler, but oh my lanta, I LOVED IT. And I was totally going to mark this book four stars because holla, the motivations were just that good! ... and then I read the last chapter. 
 You guys, I freaking *hated* the last chapter and it did ruin the book for me a little bit. If you are curious why I hated the last chapter, just hit the spoiler tag below. Otherwise, PLEASE DO NOT READ THE NEXT PARAGRAPH! It is *VERY* spoilery, and if you do not want to be spoiled, I highly suggest you do not read it! 
 So, chapter Forty-six starts with "My goddess was gone for good..." which is part of Chase's manuscript. I tolerate writers in books, but I *hate* when I get the end of a book and it seems like a character in the freaking book wrote the story. Which I think wasn't Mancusi's point, but still: I freaking hated that Chase is writing his auto-biography. He goes on to say "Not a dry eye in the house. I think it could be a best seller." I just rolled my eyes at this point. This chapter is so ridiculous! It sums up what happens after Chase and Peyton go back to the colony after finding her dad, and I would rather experience what happens, instead of getting a status report back. This chapter totally ruined the book for me and just rereading it while writing this review makes me angry. Hated it so hard.  
 While this book was good, there were parts that annoyed me that I couldn't get past. I would recommend Tomorrow Land to fans of science fiction, definitely.

Inferno tries to do toy with and follow the Robert-Langdon-thriller template at the same time. 
 So, we get a series of clues and mysteries involving art pieces and chases and narrow escapes: so much, so template. But we start out with Robert Langdon in a hospital for a brain injury, complete with amnesia: a new approach. The plot twists and turns and red herring characters abound. But this time, religion is only superficially part of the story, and there is no real conspiracy. 
 The novel entertains. It does not have the wow factor of Da Vinci Code, nor does it ever build up a sinister atmosphere, but it's fairly entertaining. Robert Langdon is still a walking, talking exposition delivery mechanism, we get flashbacks aplenty and much of the book consists of people explaining art / history at each other (though only half-heartedly, compared to earlier novels). 
 The writing is pedestrian and bland, as usual, drifting into the very-annoying through overuse of "?!" and "!?" as punctuation in dialogue and thoughts. Most characters end up sounding like teenagers on the internet as a result of that flaw, and it feels like they only barely escape from exclaiming OMG and WTF. 
 I found myself rooting for the baddie for most of the novel, to be honest, as they guy is right about many things. 
 Enjoyable popcorn entertainment, at least.

Such a bloody brilliant book! Flying five star. 
 It is so odd. So wrong. So, god, perfect. Bloody perfect. 
 I am 100% speechless. 
 Let me try to make sense for a second, before I go all "kyaa" again. 
 First of all, this book needs a good blurb, if it were not recommended to me; I would never ever pick this up. 
 Moving on, just do not focus on the spanking-bdsm-D/s themes going on in the book. Yes, sure it is hot, as it is supposed to be. But this book is just not that. It is a coming out -coming age- story. Basically a love story between a teacher and student, right? So what makes this one tick? 
 The messed up characters. The authenticity in them. The manipulative teacher. Using his age and years as an advantage against Sev. And Sev, just on the brink of his adult life; does not know how to swim in deep waters. He fails. Over and over again. Tries again, learns, and tries again. To win. Because he is young, he is able to make mistakes. 
 You do not need pages after pages of inner dialogue for character development. This book proves that. Even the side characters are not forgotten. 
 I thought Stalker did not live up the its potential. Yet everything that did not work on that book, works here. The quick pace; quirkiness of the characters. Eagerness of Sev is balanced out with reluctance of Caleb. The assault is balanced out with the wrongdoing of Caleb as a teacher. 
 The parallel between Caleb and Sev. 
 One of the best reads in 2016 and will probably be one of the all time favorites.

Just like the synopsis, this story is about two different types of people, people who bleed red, and people who bleed silver. Not only are the silvers top of society but they also have abilities or 'gifts' such as controlling metal, fire, water, reading minds and other types of abilities. For the reds in society, they are poor, live in terrible conditions, slaves to the silvers and when you turn 18 you are sent to the front of the battle lines or help win the war unless you maintain a job. Mare Barrow is a red, with no job and about to turn 18. One day she runs in a man named Cal who gets her a job as a server to the royal silvers. This is where she discovers a power of her own, the ability to control electricity. 
 Now if you haven't read Red Rising by Pierce Brown this story will be original, amazing, and one of a kind. BUT if you have read Red Rising, then Red Queen will feel like the same story told from a female viewpoint. Red Queen had an interesting concept and was a good book for what it was, but because I read Red Rising, and thoroughly enjoyed it, it felt like a rip-off. Which I'm sure was not Victoria Aveyard's intention, it is just very similar on a lot of points. Even the saying in the story - Red Rising at Dawn. 
 Now with that aside, the writing was beautiful, fast-paced, and very well detailed. Victoria did a great job explaining in great detail the characters and their surroundings. 
 I won't be continuing on with this series.

The Look has been a book that has been sitting on my shelf for a while. I always intended to pick it up, but other books got in the way. In an attempt to tackle my TBR Pile, and also read some books for authors attending YALC and forthefringe, I picked up The Look in a quiet weekend and made a start on it. 
 Within a few pages of The Look I was laughing, some of the things Ted (Edwina) comes out with had me in stitches. 
 "I think I'm supposed to 'take a sad song and make it better', but that's beyond my musical ability. 
 [Page 4] 
 When I began reading The Look I thought that it would be a difficult book for me to read, but I was glad to see that a lot of the focus was on Ted's modelling career, with some focus on Ava's battle with cancer, how she is coping, the effects of all the treatment, and how their family life is affected by this change. 
 One thing, along with Ted's humour, that I liked was how Ava uses cancer as an excuse to get Ted to do things and it is something I can relate to. My Dad this to me all the time, getting me to run up the shop for sugar for drinks even though I don't take it, running into the supermarket for him, and it brought up some happy memories of my Dad. This made the characters even more real to me, and I found it easy to relate to and empathise with them. 
 When Ted was on modelling jobs I did feel sorry for her. Modelling isn't something she was interested in, and with Ava's coaxing found herself signed up, she is lost and completely out of her comfort zone. I wanted to pick her up and take her back home to spend time with Ava. The last job she has was not an easy one, and having to deal with it, and have grief on the phone from a friend is not the ideal situation for her, but to stand up for herself takes guts and I am proud of Ted for eventually sticking with her guns. 
 The Look was a great mix of plot lines, we have the modelling with Ted, Ava fighting cancer, and her parents stuck with what to do next or how to make it better for Ava, some times I didn't know whether to laugh or cry. The Look was a quick read and a book I could not put down, I sat and did not move till I had finished the last page. If you have yet to read a book by Sophia then this is the one you need to read.

Whew. As usual, what a ride! 
 This review is probably going to mostly be a response to a lot of the other reviews I have read of this book. I was surprised by the mediocre-to-poor response this book received. I loved it! 
 It seemed like most people's complaints fell into two categories: The break-neck pace, and Cassie's intelligence. 
 So to respond to issue 1, I have two points: 
 A. This is what the series is. It has always been this way. You're just figuring this out now? (See my roller coaster analogy in my review of book 3. This turned out to be a bit more literal in book 4.) 
 B. I think you may be taking this a little too seriously. I think these books are so cram packed full of action and adventure partly because Chance is such a skilled writer and can get away with it, and partly in parody of the genre. I'm pretty sure she's doing it on purpose, people. It's meant to be entertaining. You're meant to feel dizzy and exhausted at the end, and I think you're meant to laugh a little and say "Whoa, that was insane. And maybe a little ridiculous." It's part of the fun. It's meant to be just a little over the top. 
 C. Turns out I had a third point - there were actually about two pages (almost a full day for Cassie) where all she did was sleep, play poker and swim in the pool. This is actually more downtime than we've seen in the other three books combined. 
 As far as Cassie being "dumb as a box of hammers" as one reviewer put it: I don't really know how to respond to this, other than just to say that I disagree. I don't get that impression. I have read more than my share of TSTL heroines and I just don't think Cassie is one of them. She's leaps and bounds beyond Rachel Morgan in this area, if you ask me. I've never gotten the impression that Cassie was dumb. I actually like her a lot. I felt like she was a bit bland and one dimensional in book 1, but by book 2 she had become a very dynamic and interesting character. One of my favorites, in fact. She makes mistakes like anyone would, but I don't think she makes a disproportionate amount of stupid decisions. She's been thrust into a very overwhelming position with zero preparation or training. She has no idea what she's doing, and the people close to her (ahem, Mircea) won't tell her what's going on in order to protect her. 
 Another reviewer brought up the end of the book with the big "what's going on" reveal and used it as evidence of Cassie's dumbness that people had to explain this to her. Well, 1. This needed to be explained to the reader. I for one hadn't figured it out (I barely had time to try) and 2. It was hardly overexplained. Cassie understood immediately, and at the same time as Pritkin, I might add. He hadn't figured it out either. And it wasn't pages of people having to drill something into her head. It was just the big end-of-book reveal that every book has to have, and was done to exactly the right extent.

As a girl, Cassie believed the story her grandmother told her. She believed that her mother was the daughter of the North Wind and a failed bargain with the Polar Bear King whisked her to the ends of the earth. For years, Cassie thought that one day she might be able to rescue her mother from the troll castle. 
 Cassie knows better now. Yes, her mother is gone. But Cassie has her father and their work at the Arctic research station where they live. Focused on her research of the local polar bear population and her ambitions to become a scientist, Cassie doesn't have time for anything else--especially not fairy tales. 
 Everything Cassie has learned about the world and her own life is irrevocably changed when a polar bear speaks to her. He tells her that the stories about her mother really is alive and trapped at the end of the world. He tells Cassie that he will rescue her mother if Cassie agrees to marry him. 
 When Cassie accepts the polar bear's bargain she will embark on her own journey toward through unbelievable wonders and countless dangers that will bring her east of the sun and west of the moon as she chases her truest desires for her future in Ice (2009) by Sarah Beth Durst. 
 Ice is a retelling of the Norwegian fairy tale "East of the Sun and West of the Moon." (Which itself is reminiscent of the myth of Cupid and Pysche.) 
 Durst blends pieces from the original fairy tale and blends them with elements from Inuit culture. Ice also expands the source material to add context for the presence of a Polar Bear King with an original mythology where the polar bear (called Bear) is a shape-shifting being called a munaqsri who harvests dying souls and distributes souls to newborns. Durst masterfully brings these varied elements together to create a story that is faithful to the source material while also being utterly unique. 
 Cassie is a headstrong and decidedly modern heroine. Even when she is thrust into an unfamiliar world where magic is real, Cassie learns to adapt and manipulate situations to her advantage. While her initial decision to marry Bear is a calculated one meant to bring her mother home, Cassie's feelings evolve as she begins to imagine a previously impossible future for herself beside her new husband. 
 Ice thoughtfully explores issues of choice as Cassie is forced repeatedly to place a value on her own free will. When she is separated from Bear she faces numerous obstacles while constantly running up against the question of how much she is willing to sacrifice in her efforts to find and rescue him. In addition Ice includes a nuanced treatment of what it means to be part of a family as well as what it means to grow up--two things that are central to Cassie's character development. 
 Ice is a clever and evocative fantasy retelling. Sure to appeal to fans of the original fairy tale as well as fantasy fans in general. 
 Possible Pairings: Plain Kate by Erin Bow, Fire by Kristin Cashore, A Creature of Moonlight by Rebecca Hahn, Winterspell by Claire Legrand, A Court of Thorns and Roses by Sarah J. Maas, East by Edith Pattou, The Woman Who Loved Reindeer by Meredith Ann Pierce, The Glass Casket by McCormick Templeman

I don't remember exactly what made me add Perfect Chemistry, by Simone Elkeles, to my TBR list. Maybe that's why it was just okay for me. 
 This is a story of classes and stereotypes. Brittany Ellis looks like a perfect, wealthy, high school senior, but her life is quite the opposite. Alex Fuentes acts like a tough, unpredictable gang member. To the eye, the two have nothing in common, but when they're assigned as chemistry lab partners, sparks fly in more ways than one. Alex accepts a bet that he can have sex with Brittany before Thanksgiving, but the more he gets to know her, the more he feels for her. It doesn't take Brittany long to realize she's falling for Alex too, but she has to come to terms with how her life will change once her relationship with him is outed. They're both victims of their choices and those of their families, and some of those choices may be impossible to overcome. 
 I didn't really connect to the main characters in this book. I'm not sure if the characters didn't understand who they were as people, or if that was my problem. Both Alex and Brittany projected a certain image to the outside world that wasn't who they were, but it didn't seem like just an image. Alex didn't just want to be seen as tough, he was tough. He intimidated people and enjoyed it. He was cruel to survive. I couldn't really separate those qualities of his personality from those he exhibited when he was with his family or eventually with Brittany. And Brittany wanted people to think she was perfect, and she did a lot of things to be just that. I guess when it comes right down to it, the author never convinced me that her characters were brave enough to take the risks they took. The whole thing felt kind of contrived. 
 I liked the minor characters like Isa, Paco, and Sierra. In some ways, they were stronger than the mains, or at the very least, more believable. 
 The writing was decent but nothing that knocked me off my feet. The end of the story felt slightly rushed compared to the majority of the book. I didn't mind the alternating points of view, but I think it lent a somewhat disjointed feeling to the book, or maybe I felt that way simply because the two worlds were so vastly different. And a minor annoyance for me: I'm Canadian, so my "second language"--that's a stretch--is francais. I liked the idea of Spanish/Mexican phrases, but I so often felt lost reading them, like it was a private joke that I wasn't in on.

This year I have read some really crappy books. I mean books that I would have to set down and try to not throw the book out the window. This book was different. I would have to set down the book and try to sort out the things C.S. Lewis was trying to teach. 
 Each chapter is a short story and I can promise that one of them will really affect you. The one I related too, was the man and his red lizard. I've done things I'm not proud of and I've gotten addicted to some hardcore stuff. Everyone would tell me to just quit, but it's not that easy. Your addiction literally becomes a part of you. 
 An angel sees this man and offers to help by killing the lizard. The man tells the angel that the lizard is sleeping so it will not bug him. The angel continues to press on killing the lizard which frightens the man because he's not sure if he can let go of his 'lizard'. 
 One part of the story really hit me hard: 
 'Get back! You're burning me. How can I tell you to kill it? You'd kill me if you did.' 
 'It is not so.' 
 'Why, you're hurting me now.' 
 'I never said it wouldn't hurt you. I said it wouldn't kill you.' 
 The lizard is supposed to represent lust but I feel that it can represent any type of addiction. Humans grab onto whatever will make them happy and when it comes time to let go, it's hard. We go through relapse and continue to mess up. Does it kill us? No. Does it hurt us? Yes. 
 My favorite part of that chapter is when the slimy lizard turns into the beautiful horse. The man has rid himself of his addiction and is able to turn from weak to strong. 
 You don't have to be a Christian in order to understand this book. C.S. Lewis is such a wise man that sometimes what he says goes right through you, only to hit you hard hours later. That's alright though. You'll gain something in the end. 
 Highly recommended.

How in the hell am I supposed to review this book. 
 Amazing. 
 Incredible. 
 Unique. 
 Fascinating. 
 I got this gorgeous ARC at BEA this year and Its been staring at me from my bookshelves since JUNE you guys!! 
 I finally said F&%K it and grabbed it because I was sick of seeing everyone talking about the awesomeness inside its pages. 
 I can't even imagine how to explain it to you though. 
 Illuminae tells the story of the destruction of the Kerenza colony... this happened one year ago from where the story begins. As the reader you are presented with interviews, medical reports, ship schematics, emails, personal messages, journal pages and ship communications to tell the full story. 
 And what a story it is. 
 At the heart of Illuminae is a bit of a love story... I found myself so enthralled with both Ezra and Kady that I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. But seriously can we talk for a second about Ezra??? I have a bit of a crush on him myself I mean page 116 solidified that. And Kady is super smart and a total hacker which I loved. 
 But there's more than that... A mutating plague has attacked the survivors of the Kerenza colony who are trapped on the remaining ships... and Kady and Ezra find themselves separated and desperate to find out the truth to what is happening to those around them. 
 And then there is also AIDAN - he is the ships Artificial Intelligence and it's hard to tell what his ultimate goal is here. I mean if you've seen 2001 A Space Odyssey you know all about H.A.L. and what he did, and at times throughout you kind of question whether AIDAN has gone crazy, but the rationale the AI uses ultimately makes sense when you look at its actions through a lens with no emotion. 
 Though this book is ginormous... 599 pages, you will steamroll right through them because I guarantee you won't want to put this down once you start it. And of course Kristoff and Kaufman will leave you begging for the next book, which can't come soon enough. I do want to offer a bit of a side note... this story has a lot of violence so if that's not quite your thing, maybe be forewarned on that aspect. If you can get past that, I think you're going to love the crazy and unique story that these authors have created. 
 Pre-order this, put your name on the library waitlist, whatever you have to do to get it in your hands as quick as possible do it. You're not going to want to miss out on this when it releases. 
 Thank you Random House for having these at BEA!!

As a whole, I've enjoyed The Underland Chronicles. However, I do find myself a little disappointed that almost every series or trilogy ends with a grand war. Or more specifically, a last book where a single war takes up the entire plot. Yes, it does make for compelling reading and I was engaged the whole time, but I feel like it's somehow . . . wrong (?) to need all this violence in order to craft intensity for the climax (i.e. the last book). It also seems like a Collins trademark now, her last books need to be ridiculously war-centered with way too much gore and killing. 
 This aspect certainly seemed overdone in Gregor and the Code of Claw. I couldn't tell you how much imagery included blood dripping, spurting, running down and mixing with someone else's blood, seeping, etc. Not to mention this is for a young audience. I feel in order to create this emotional and action-packed potency she needed to make everything as violent as possible, and it made me feel like she lost track of the children she was writing for. There was even a scene where a rat ripped the head off another. It just seemed like too much, like she's feeding the stereotype that children need action and violence to be entertained. There certainly was a lot of that here. 
 All that aside, though, it wasn't all bad. I enjoyed Lizzie's role, and the softer side of Ripred. I felt like the relationship between Luxa and Gregor became a bit planned and awkward (including making Luxa's role "smaller" because she needed to be protected all the time since she was a woman and beloved by the male protagonist, despite her skill). 
 But all in all this series has some beautiful moments and great story lines that I enjoyed.

I loved this book right from the start. It starts off with a bang, with so much going on, that I was sucked in immediately - desperately wanting to figure out what was going on. The writing remained exquisite, the world incredibly well developed, and the characters continued to grow. 
 I will say that while I LOVED this book and I am giving it 5 stars, I do think it is a bit of a filler book. And that opinion is simply based on the ending. There were two climatic moments towards the end. The first I will call the er... 'journey climax.' This one was okay. It wasn't particularly shocking BUT I did love the character growth it allowed for Elisa and for Storm. The second moment was the 'back home climax' and that one was disappointing. The book on a whole had me wildly guessing and expecting a big twist, which never really happened. 
 That said, I was still flailing around at the ending with FEELS because of ELISA AND HECTOR. 
 Let me tell you a story about shipping. I don't get wrapped up in it THAT often. Don't get me wrong, I have some HARDCORE OTPs and when I ship, I ship hard. But recently I have only really been flailing over Captain Swan. I love Chaol and Celaena but I'm not crazy obsessed. I love the tension between Alina and the Darkling, while hoping that Bardugo gives us some great Alina and Sturmhond. But I'm pretty chill about it. 
 Elisa and Hector though? I AM OBSESSED. I AM IN LOVE. I WANT MORE. I WANT EVERYTHING. I think part of the reason they hit me so hard is that they are built slowly and so well. The foundation is there from the first book but it is built up bit by bit again here. Lots of little looks and touches that have you yearning and then then...AND THEN. They had me squealing on a public train, which was a little bit embarrassing, and I am not ashamed to admit they were my favourite part of this book. I think that if you don't feel this relationship, you'll be a little more disappointed with the lack of plot...BUT HOW CAN YOU NOT FEEL THEIR RELATIONSHIP? GUHHH. 
 There ARE other things to love about this book though, and it really does come down to the characters for me. Storm was a great addition, as was FELIX. Rosario continued to be even cuter than EVER. Hector. Hector. Hector. But lets talk about the ladies... 
 Elisa continues to grow, but at a steadier rate than the first book. A lot of people struggled with the religious aspect of the first book and that is still prevalent here. However, it seems pretty clear to me Elisa is going to find out that her beliefs are not all she thought they were. It's not a straight forward thing with God absolutely being the right course here. I'm really intrigued to see how that ends. 
 MARA. I love Mara a huge amount. And I just have to mention a wonderful scene where Mara and Elisa talk about losing her virginity. It was just a great scene to see in a YA book. Mara is totally chill about saying it doesn't matter that her first time wasn't amazing...it's just a first time. It doesn't mean all that much. As long as its safe and respectful. PERFECT. 
 I also ADORED what happened with Ximena in this book, and it goes back to my point about the religous aspects in this series not being all they are made out to be. There is no question that she loves Elisa, but her actions and choices become so incredibly frustrating. The scene near the end was perfect growth and storytelling. I think she is a very complex, which means great,character. 
 I'll be honest, I'm whizzing through this review so I can continue reading. I am going to jump straight into the final. I expect it to give me all the feels that this book did, but with an even greater plot.

"Shiver" by Maggie Stiefvater left me torn and undecided, and I am lost somewhere between adoration and disgust. 
 The book holds a certain tone of beautiful heart shattering melancholy, and it has a ghostly atmosphere of sadness and loss. The writing contains vivid imagery, and made me feel cold on a warm spring day. 
 The story is by no means a realistic account of true feelings, it is rather a lyrical tale of a poetical love. The dialogue isn't witty or even believable - but it is stunning. 
 On the other hand, there is almost no plot at all. The majority of the pages are "wasted" on sincere descriptions of a deep love, and when something dramatic actually is happening it seems misplaced and wrong. 
 Grace and Sam do not feel real; they're just pretty reflections of Stiefvater's artistic phrases. And their surroundings feel flat and tame; Stiefvater does not really describe anything else but Grace and Sam, their love, their heartache and the atmosphere in the woods. 
 I adore Stiefvater's writing, her compositions and her words, but I despise her simple story and her lack of characterization. Sam does not feel convincing. Grace is highly illogical. And their thoughts blend together in a hazy blur, so it's impossible to tell them apart. They do not have individual personalities, they only have each other and their mutual love.

 A meandering trip though mountains and across deserts from China to Istanbul, and then into the war between Prussia and France. The summons to leave China is suspicious and never fully explained, the circumstances in Istanbul are suspicious but never fully explored, and the battles are messy, disorganized, and demoralizing defeats--that part is probably the most realistic. 
 Parts of the story should have been more detailed and explored with more depth; that lack of detail and depth weakens the overall book. And yet, Laurence and Temeraire continue to be wonderful and engaging characters, and some of the secondary characters, like Granby, Tharkay, Keynes, and even the Chinese cook, Gong Su, help fill out the story. There are only a few dragon characters with whom we spend any time--Lien and Arkady chief among them, with a cameo by Iskierka. 
 All in all, a weaker installment in the Temeraire series. I hope the subsequent books return to the tighter plotting and writing of first book in the series.

One of my reading objectives this year is to revisit some (as many as I can, really) of the Stephen King books that I read more than a decade ago, just as a way to reconnect with one of my favorite authors. I began with Gerald's Game, which I believe is one of King's most underrated works. The entire narrative is pervaded by a sense of desolation and desperation and is brilliantly crafted. The tension that he creates with such small details (a glass of water, for instance) is absolutely masterful. This book is graphic and gory and disturbing on a very visceral level, but for some reason, I love it. I think because, at its core, it's a very feminist work, which is completely unexpected.

These books are kind of like my 'break' books between others. I enjoy them for the easy read, a familiar pattern I can rely on and it's easy to slide back into these characters. I found Uprooted a rather nice twist on Dante. The opening line of the Inferno goes something like "In the middle of my life, I found myself in a dark wood wandering/ for the straight way was lost." And boy, oh, boy, is that a dark wood in Agnieszka's valley. Terrifying and enchanting. I especially liked the source of its evil and how it related to the enchantment on the Dragon's castle. 
 Middle-aged grumpy Dragon subs for Dante and his Beatrice is Agnieszka, and she proves to be the active protagonist and a lot more interesting than Dante's muse. 
 I liked the book and thought it was well-written, but I could almost hear Novik's agent telling her to keep the story moving. Chapters end on cliff-hangers, which is not bad in itself, even if Dan Brown has overused it and given it a bad name. But there were a lot of times when I would have liked to dive deeper into the way magic worked and into the complicated relationship between the Dragon and Agnieszka instead of rushing off to the next crisis. The end result of this rushing was that the Dragon never became three-dimensional to me, though I thought he had a lot of potential to be a profoundly interesting character. 
 Ok, ok, I'm caviling. Honestly, once Prince Marek appeared on the scene and they went into the Wood to get the Queen, it moved along very well and I had trouble putting it down. 
 There was a discussion in the Science Fiction and Fantasy group about whether or not this is YA. There was some dislike of the sex scenes, which were few, IMHO, and well-written and certainly not too much for YA. My writers' group has a very talented writer of paranormal YA. She stops at the bedroom door, so to speak, but doesn't shy away from the fact that much of her audience is probably sexually active. Heck, I remember that many years ago, an elementary school librarian gave my nine year old daughter a book, Spider's Voice, which tells the story of Abelard and Heloise from the POV of a mute who is himself castrated, if I remember the story correctly. This necessitated some very delicate discussion when my daughter came asking about...um...er...what they did to Abelard. The book looked like a middle grade book, had a middle grade sort of cover, and without her questions I would never have known. So there you go. 
 Anyway, all that to say that Uprooted doesn't come close Lev Grossman's or GRR Martin's adult fantasies, which are full of sex. I wouldn't have hesitated to recommend this to my daughter in high school. It would have seemed tame to her, I'm sure.

Starship Troopers, when you boil it down is a military journal. It is an account of Rico's trials and tribulations as he climbs through the ranks in the Mobile Infantry. The characters are not overly well defined, the plot meanders and at times seems to have decided to not show up for a particular chapter, and yet, the story as a whole never once failed to keep me reading. 
 The settings and weapons are the most descript portions of the story and yet I never found myself asking Heinlein to get on with it. 
 I've read a few reviews of this novel myself and several of them have criticized the book for its lack of a romantic thread, but in my opinion, it doesn't need one. Heinlein made it clear that his protagonist was a man and that he not only noticed women but felt a strong desire to have them in his life - more so to remember what he was fighting for, but it is not as though the character completely ignored the female sex. 
 Two other criticisms claim the novel is militaristic, or that it has a fascist agenda. This novel is about a futuristic military power - of course it's going to be pro military - Heinlein was creating what he saw as a potential for a perfect society. In his opinion that meant a place where proven dedication to the greater good was the only means by which to gain citizenship - but it certainly didn't mean a lack of war. I can see where the fascist thoughts arise because the book is so militarily focused and if you really want to get into it, I'm sure there are dozens of forums out there that will gladly accommodate you. 
 Overall I enjoyed the novel immensely.

Williams never seizes to amaze me. I love every one of her books; this on is no exception. I was shocked by the turn of events though. And I'm having some thoughts on a bigger picture here...

Evie O'Neill is making the move from small-town Ohio to New York City. Her unusual gift (and her mouth) has forced her family to send her to live with her uncle until things blow over. Uncle Will runs The Museum of American Folklore, Superstition, and the Occult (or The Museum of the Creepy Crawlies as it's known around town), with the help of his assistant Jericho. As Evie begins her stay in 1920's NYC, she has dreams of fabulous parties and adventures to last a lifetime. What she doesn't count on is a supernatural stirring that is taking over the city. When a series of grusome murders seems tied to some sort of cult, Will is asked to help (and Evie, not to be left out, tags along). She soon realizes that the gift that got her exiled from Ohio could actually help catch a dangerous and evil murderer. 
 With an incredible cast of characters, The Diviners gives readers a mystery and so much more! 
 My Thoughts: 
 I read this book for book club, so if it wasn't for that I probably never would have picked it up. It's so far outside of my comfort zone that I just don't seeing it ever getting on my radar. I mean it's Historical Fiction AND Supernatural... two genres I generally never read. Maybe because this was so different from my usual, or maybe just because the writing was so awesome, I found myself loving it right away!! 
 I have never read a Libba Bray book before, but I can pretty much guarantee this won't be the last. I didn't read much of the synopsis before I started, so I went in pretty much blind. I read one page and I was like "oh this is in the 20's??" and I wanted to quit. There's just something about Historical Fiction that just turns me off. But I pushed through... oh woah, I am so glad I did. It got SO interesting and even though the book is huge (578 pages), I flew through them because I was hooked. 
 My favorite part of this book was all the characters. Normally a book with so many main and side characters would have me confused. Somehow that didn't happen at all here. Every character had a story and a purpose. And they were all so memorable. You have troublemaker Sam, flapper/Ziegfeld girl Theta, sensible Mabel, strong and silent Jericho, sensitive Memphis, thick-headed Isaiah, set-in-his-ways Will, blind homeless Bill, good guy Henry... and of course head-strong Evie and so many more. And I loved them all! (Ok Jericho was kind of a yawn for me, but still...) My favorite was Memphis, but I don't think I'm alone in this. Hello!! Smart, sensitive guy who writes poetry and can heal people?? What more do you want? Evie, however, was something else. I enjoyed having her as the main character, but it's hard not to have a love-hate feeling towards her. She was such a smart-ass!! Especially for the time period! But at the same time I respected her courage and related to her inability to hold her emotions in. Her immaturity could definitely turn some people off, but she had enough redeeming qualities that I think people will be able to like her eventually. 
 I could tell this novel was the product of a ton of research. The way the era and city was painstakingly described was definitely a high point of this book for me. The atmosphere totally captured my imagination and has me wanting to read more about the history of New York. Some of the dialogue seemed a little forced and irked me at times, but all the "and how"'s, "giggle water"'s, and "pos-i-tute-ly"'s had me grinning most of the time. 
 If I could point out an observation about this book it would be that it seemed very adult. It's not the subject-matter or anything like that, it's just.... something. A feeling that I have that it's written more for adults who read YA than it is teen readers. I could be totally off base, but even my book club mentioned it, so it's not just me who's feeling it. Maybe it's because most of the characters are either adults or teens who live adult lives or maybe it's just the vibe I got, but something about it gave me the teens-won't-like-this-as-much feeling. 
 Bottom line: I can't wait to read the sequel! I look forward to seeing if/when these Diviners team up to defeat evil!!! 
 OVERALL: WOW! Definitely a favorite for me. I never read Historical Fiction, but this one made me want to try out more of them. It's one part mystery, one part paranormal, and one part historical.... and all parts creepy and addicting! Definitely a recommended read from me. 
 My Blog:
I always appreciate a fantasy story that doesn't channel Tolkein too much. I was impressed too by how young the author is.

This was the first post of my weekly literature blog on tumblr. 
 I come from a country where fantasy is third class fiction. It's not really literature. It's regarded as cheap escapism. And yet I was drawn to it and thought that it had a potential to express what reality-based books fail to convey. Unfortunately, there are a lot of books in this genre that can't quite live up to literary standards. I was growing tired of the recurring, poorly executed themes, of the lack of authenticity. (Authenticity in fantasy? -Yes!) 
 With 'The Name of the Wind' Patrick Rothfuss has created a book that is an ode to life and that restored my faith in fantasy. It celebrates life in all its beauty - music, poetry, knowledge, the pleasure of crafting something with your own two hands, the complexity of human interaction, the delight of going off into the unknown, the fascination of different cultures and different ways of thinking - and for me, it includes in this beauty also the 'darker' aspects of loss, loneliness, not knowing how to pay your rent, let alone your university tuition fees next semester. Oh - and silence. And I don't even mean the silence in three parts, which commences and ends each of the books in the series. This is merely synonymous for a greater delight that I find in these books: yes, Kvothe, our young protagonist, is quite exceptional, constantly in trouble and stumbling through many extraordinary adventures, yet the Kingkiller Chronicle has what many other fantasy tomes are lacking: an appreciation of the small things and the quiet moments between the big bangs. 
 I doubt that I am truly able to bring across what I so love about Patrick Rothfuss' writing. I discovered him around the time when I started to come out of my shell, to change my guarded attitude to that of embracing the small beauties in life, of encountering people with a smile and an open heart, and of daring to take risks (such as going abroad), and I found a soulmate in these books. 
 Snuggle up in bed with a big pot of coffee or tea and a jar of biscuits beside you and enjoy!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Where to start... 
 I couldn't put it down, again. Now I'm so flipping tired. So this one picks up in District 13, which was predictable after the two kids in the woods in Catching Fire. But...without Peeta. 
 Gr. I didn't like that, but I got why it was done. I mean, the entire series so far has revolved around her protecting people: Prim, herself, then Peeta. Always Peeta. And now that she can't... Oh. And those scenes where Katniss goes crazy? Loved them. I felt a little crazy myself. But it's good to show that Katniss is affected by everything going on, all the death and realizing that Peeta is being tortured to break her. I felt helpless, so that's good writing, buck-os. 
 Plus, with Peeta gone, we get more Gale. She even tries to give it a go with him when Peeta comes back and she writes him off as insane, which was awesome--we needed that to realize that even if it wasn't his bomb in the end, they wouldn't have been happy. The scene where she fantasizes about what could have happened if she wasn't reaped was spot on. But those things did happen, and it changed her. Gale doesn't understand the changes it made in Katniss--she's seen so much destruction and it damages her, while Gale is almost immune to it. That's part of the reason why she needed to be with Peeta, imho. 
 There were a couple times I shed a few tears. My boyfriend kept looking at me funny, but whatever. Like when Katniss figured out why Snow had Peeta; Finnick (Sheesh that one was a surprise) dying even after he just got Annie!; and then Prim....ugh. My heart stopped. 
 That scene confused me. But I think that jumpy narration is perfect for the series, because it'd be pointless to show her watching people stampede in--and boring. So the exposition giving it away was nice. The shock she felt, the mental retreat, was spot on. I felt it with her. I mean, the entire revolution started when she volunteered to save Prim--and then for Coin, the president of the rebels, to kill her? I don't know how Katniss even recovered. 
 Ok, Katness now. I dig her. She's not perfect, in the slightest. She doesn't listen, she is indecisive, she doesn't really know herself (she's a teen--that's natural). I don't think she ever led on both Gale and Peeta, she just would need comfort which is totally understandable. And she wasn't with either of them, too. Actually, I saw her kissing Peeta more out of choice, while when she kissed Gale it was always to comfort him. It just wasn't as romantic on her side towards him, in my opinion. That "warm" feeling (haha) only arrived with Peeta, if I remember it right. 
 Ok, now the end..... How the hell she wrapped up the Peeta/Katniss relationship bothered me. There should have been more confrontation before suddenly the line, "we grew together." Uh...huh? That's not a good way to wrap up the romance, but I got it. Katniss was damaged, so was Peeta. They kind of had to re-learn how to function with each other. And I liked how a lot of what Peeta said in the first book was reiterated here, but his meaning more clear. That was perfect. I just wanted a little more grandiose when they finally got together. But I did like the last line of, "You love me. Real or not real?" Because it stays true to Katniss: she would never have admitted it without Peeta to push her. Gale and her would have been a little emotionless in that sense, because it was always Peeta who made that emotion come out. 
 I dunno. I loved it. I didn't want it to end but I couldn't put it down. Now I dunno what to read.

Faithful Place made all sorts of Ten Best lists in 2010, for novels in general, not just mystery. It's one of those mysteries in which the whodunit is subservient to the character development and the ambiance. It is set in contemporary Dublin, where narrator Frank Mackie is an undercover cop, estranged from his dysfunctional family for 20 years. He returns to his family and neighborhood when his former lover Rosie's suitcase and later her body shows up, 20 years after he assumed she ditched him on the night of their planned elopement. 
 This is a good read, very atmospheric, with Irish-tinged dialog so vivid you'll almost think you're listening to an audiobook! The reader's heart goes out to Frankie, so damaged by his upbringing amid poverty and alcoholism, and trying hard to be a good father to his own daughter. The resolution of the plot is not particularly surprising, but that is not particularly important, either.

This was a sad story. Period. There is no sugar coating to a book that revolves about the suicide of one girl, and the thirteen reasons that drove her to make that decision. It's a book that shows you the hard truth, that in a sensitive situation, almost anything could be the last straw, that one final nail that would seal the coffin. Some of the reasons that Hanna stated in her tale could have been ignored if there where just a singular event, like the ass grabbing thing that happened right at the beginning. It doesn't mean that it's not a sexual abuse, and it doesn't mean it's any less humiliating that anything else that happened to her, but if it was just that, just a single event, she could have made it pass that.  
 We listen to the tapes with Clay, and to be honest, I felt as sick as he did the more I advanced. Hannah tells her story in a very simple manner. She tells you exactly why it happened, because she has nothing to lose anymore. She knows she'll be dead soon, so why not bare it all? 
 It broke my heart to read all the reasons, to listen how with each day that passed she cracked even more, until she couldn't hold it together anymore. All the signs were there, but no one saw them because it was easier to ignore her than try to help. But I can't judge anyone about those 'obvious' signs, because sometimes it's not that obvious, and anyone that knows someone that killed themselves knows that. 
 She's been through a lot, and she gave up. And when she recorded her story, Hannah knew it was the end. That by the time anyone would hear it, she would be gone. And on the other side, we read Clay's reaction to her story. We read the horror and the pain, the emotions that took over him and made it nearly impossible for him to finish listening to her. And toward the end, it got harder for me to keep reading the book as well, because she was always so honest about what had happened to her, and it just broke my heart even more. 
 I feel like everyone should read this book, because it had such an important message and maybe it will help someone to stop a friend from taking their own life.

I kept changing my mind about the rating, but I think three stars is what it deserves. This story has a lot of problems, and I don't think I can blame the translator this time. I think this all falls on Yoshimoto. 
 The Lake is about an artist named Chihiro who is assigned the job of painting a mural for a struggling school, but her integrity is challenged by the corporation funding her and that instills some personal drama. She's also just started a new relationship with the emotionally distant Nakajima, who she's been going all "Rear Window" on by spying on him across the street. But he's a brooding mess. Oh does he brood! Then he takes her to his "family" and broods some more. Then the book ends with this sort of revelation about why he broods & then I brooded about why I even liked the lady who wrote this. 
 This is Yoshimoto's longest book, but boy did it feel longer. I think she was attempting to write something more like a novel in length. What ends up happening is she circles around the same problems, in the same scene, over and over, until you want to puke. The summary of the book is also misleading, because the Japanese cult that "inspired" this tepid mess is mentioned in the last 30 or so pages and doesn't really deliver anything exciting. I know her books aren't meant to be exciting like that, but she relies too much on Nakajima's past without using it to her advantage. So he's angry because of this cult, which doesn't even get discussed properly, and we don't explore why or what specifically happened. It's all ambiguous, and the book should have explored Nakajima's past a lot more than it did, instead of hiding it like it was some great surprise. 
 The beginning and end of the book had a lot of promise, but the 80% that made up the middle just felt like filler. Despite some nice poetic phrases and descriptions, which is the only reason this book didn't get one star, I was bored. And I think the translator could have done a better job. Some of the prose came out staggered like this: 
 "I feel bad. This is why I feel bad. In conclusion, I feel bad." 
 I think it's safe to say she didn't intend it to sound like that, and it could've been consolidated. This happened in another recent book of hers I read, but the book didn't rely solely on her prose so I didn't mind it as much. So this is really a one star book, but because Yoshimoto can emote something in one sentence that some writers need pages to convey, I gave it three. I just wish the plot that inspired these prose was more fascinating.

ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL. 
 BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS. 
 This must be the highest point of honesty that we can reach. Because it doesn't just apply to animals, it applies to humans as well. Better, if you want my opinion. 
 This is, if you have much imagination, a really scary book. Let's say, for the sake of argument, that hypothetically this could happen. I'd shit my pant. I've lived my whole life thinking that even though in an animal there is a soul, there is not enough intelligence to resemble what I, as a human being, can do. What if one day I find out that that's not the case? Huh?! I'd probably run for the hills and start living in a cave. 
 What George Orwell has a lot of is humor. His jokes wouldn't be funny in meaningless contexts, but in Animal Farm, everything he did had a purpose - that of showing us how not so different we are from them. For that, he used satire and a lot of figures of speech, and he managed to create a world we could believe in. 
 It's still scary, though.

This is a solid story by Sara B. Larson. 
 I enjoyed getting to know Alex/a, her brother, and her love interests. Everyone who know me knows I'm a sucker for cross-dressing/gender-bending stories where the female lead must dress as a male in order to fulfill her dream (fighter, join the army) or to keep her alive (escape from rape houses, as was in the case of Defy). 
 What makes me giddy is when the male lead learns of the deception. Did he always know? Was he fighting an attraction to a boy? All stories in this genre get an automatic comparison to "These Old Shades" by Georgette Heyer. Which, if I'm being honest, is one of the best girl-pretends-to-be-a-boy novels. Not many newer novels stack up against a Heyer novel. So I'll just move on. 
 I know many objected to the rape houses (reviewers) in Defy, and I wasn't a fan of them, either. Other than the plot catalyst to make Alexa become Marcel's "brother", the rape houses (aka Breeding Houses) really didn't add to the plot overall. Thankfully we only see inside the rape house once, but it is talked of a lot (men buttoning their breeches as they leave the rape house). It certainly leaves an impression... 
 I guess I just didn't see the point. It would take years for any children born of the breeding houses to become soldiers, or, if a female child, to be raised as "incubators" until their monthly courses came. So, for the sake of argument, it would take 13 years for this to take affect... 
 Eh, I could have done without all of that, and I would have rather seen a different reason for Alexa to become Alex. 
 There were a few times that I wanted to slap Alexa. When everyone knows her as Alex, she's a fucking badass. But when others realize/learn she's a female, she becomes...dunno...not a badass? I get it. The author needed us to see that, on the inside, Alexa is vulnerable and has no idea of how to be a female. But the essence that made her her shouldn't have changed all that much. 
 Between her two suitors, I'm team Rylan all the way. Sorry Princey-poo. I could have done without the love triangle, and the semi-insta-love between Alexa and Prince Damien. I'm still of the opinion that he's only using her. 
 Overall, parts dragged, parts were exciting, and the fighting was good, and I kept reading because I really wanted to know what happened next! For that, 3.5 stars. I'll pick up Ignite when it's in the 4.99 range. Right now, as I write this review, it's 9.99. A bit too high for my e-book buying range.

 Cadence Miller grew up in a Christian family. Ten months ago, she was involved in a robbery, with other teenagers, while high in cocaine. This led her to ten months of juvenile detention. This changes everything for her when she came back to school. Almost everyone in school started bullying her. She also lost her friends and her parents' trust, 
 While cleaning the streets during detention, Cadence met Mark Connelly. When she came back to school, she discovered that he is her math teacher. They fell in love and entered in a secret relationship (which includes a sexual relationship). 
 Good also showed Cadence's point of view on Christianity, and how she interpreted the Word of God, and how she let it affect her decisions and her relationship with Mark who has different beliefs compared to hers. This also twisted her beliefs in some way. In some parts of the story, I saw that instead of her Christian beliefs affecting her relationship, it was her relationship that affected her beliefs.

When I started reading this book, I thought "ok, this is starting out like 3 other YA books that I've read". Teenage girl with a somewhat traumatic life, shipped off to another school where she meets a boy who has her mesmerized. Even though I was tempted to stop reading this, thinking this was going to be like the others, I'm glad I stuck with it. 
 Emma's living with her Aunt, after escaping a death at the hands of her drunken step father. She's enrolled it a very posh private school, where her aunt is on the board and her younger cousin is her only ally amongst the student body. When she meets Brendan Salinger, she doesn't expect her reaction. 
 "He turned and looks at me for a brief second - any my pulse sped. I didn't expect my response. I'd been around good looking guys before -- but this guy looked like a rock star. Long black lashes framed his green eyes - twinkling green eyes that locked with mine." 
 I like that Emma had issues fitting in at the new school. She didn't fit into any of the pre-established "cliques" and didn't really try, figuring out what the dynamics were at the school pretty quickly. She did manage to make friends with the "outcast" Angelique, when no one else would because she was a scholarship student. I also like the fact that even though Emma felt drawn to Brendan, she wasn't overly obsessive about him (which could have very easily happened). 
 Brendan was one of those male characters that we all wished we had as our first (and true) love in high school. Once he stopped running from what he was feeling, he was the boyfriend that made his girlfriend feel like a princess. He was protective, but not in the "I'm going to put you in a bubble" sense. Even when he knew that the two of them being together could be disastrous for Emma, he admitted he wasn't willing to let her go. 
 The story did have it's villans and they were spectacular in a high school kind of way. Kristin was the ultimate bitch and made sure to make Emma's life a living hell. How dare she snag the hot guy! And we can't forget about Anthony. He was evil, in every sense of the word. 
 Sprinkle in a little magic, some century old curses and plain old high school woes and you've got yourself quite an enjoyable read. I recommend this one.

Hounded was awesome. It was full of action, humor, fantasy, and mythology that was insanely fun to read. I devoured it in a short amount of time, raving about it to others the entire time. It was such a cool mixture of old mythology and lore with modern times. Atticus, a 2100 year old Druid, had such a good grip on today's world. His sense of humor was awesome and his narration kept me turning the pages. 
 Hounded had all sorts of mythological elements. Atticus was a Druid, lived in a town with witches, had a Viking vampire for a lawyer, and was friendly with a werewolf pack. He was visited by the Morrigan, an old Celtic goddess (but the sort of goddess who would NOT appreciate being called old!) and just about every other legend, god, or creature existed in this world. Demons, faeries (the terrifying kind), even Mary. I loved how the author created such a universe. It never would have occurred to me to have a world where every religion was true to some degree. 
 Atticus definitely made the story. He could communicate with his Irish wolfhound, which was hilarious because his dog was awesome. He fit in with college kids, but his insight and narration had me cracking up. He made the best references ever. "These are not the Druids you're looking for" came out of his mouth at one point, which is basically awesome. As Atticus fought a powerful Celtic god, his dog was commenting on the action and made South Park references that had me laughing. 
 Overall, Hounded was one of the most fun books I've read all year. It's definitely a must read for any geek and any lover of a fun fantasy book.
